The Prophet ﷺ prescribed for the one who purifies himself, after finishing ablution, that he recite the testimony and then say: "O God, make me of those who repent, and make me of those who purify themselves." Thus the ranks of purity were perfected for him, inwardly and outwardly.

For by the testimony he purifies himself from shirk, by repentance he purifies himself from sins, and by water he purifies himself from outward filth. So he prescribed the most complete ranks of purity before entering upon God and standing before Him. When he was purified outwardly and inwardly, he was permitted to enter upon Him by standing before Him, since he had freed himself from fleeing (from his master) by coming to His house and the place of his servitude.

For this reason, coming to the mosque is, in the view of some, a completion of the servitude of the obligatory prayer, and in the view of others, of the recommended prayer. The servant, in his state of heedlessness, is like a runaway slave from his Lord, having left his limbs and heart idle from the service for which he was created. When he comes to Him, he has returned from his flight. When he stands before Him in the station of servitude, humility and brokenness, he has summoned the compassion of his master upon him and his turning towards him after aversion.

He was commanded to face the Qibla, the Sacred House, with his face, and to face God, Mighty and Majestic, with his heart, so that he may shed what he was in of turning away and aversion. Then he stands before Him in the station of the humble, submissive, needy one who seeks the compassion of his master. He lays his hands down in submission and surrender, head bowed, heart humble, gaze lowered, his heart not turning from Him nor his gaze to right or left, rather his whole heart turned toward Him and his entire being facing Him.

Then he says the takbir with glorification and reverence, and his heart is in harmony with his tongue in the takbir. God is greater in his heart than everything. This takbir is confirmed by the fact that there is nothing in his heart greater than God that would occupy him from Him. When he is occupied with other than God, and what he is occupied with is more important to him than God, his takbir is with his tongue but not with his heart. The takbir removes him from wearing the garment of pride which is incompatible with servitude, and prevents his heart from turning to other than God, since God is greater in his heart than everything. The true meaning of saying "God is greater" and the practice of the servitude of takbir guard him against these two afflictions, which are among the greatest veils between him and God.

When he says, "Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You," and praises God with what is worthy of Him, he has emerged from heedlessness, which is also a veil between him and God, and has brought the greeting and praise that one addresses to a king upon entering his presence, as glorification, exaltation and a preface before one's need. In this praise there is so much of the courtesy of servitude that it draws His turning towards him, His good pleasure with him, and His aid in his needs.

When he begins the recitation, he precedes it with seeking refuge in God from Satan, for Satan is most eager for the servant in such a station, which is the noblest of his stations and the most beneficial to him in this world and the Hereafter. Satan is most eager to divert him from it and cut him off from it, with body and heart. If he cannot cut him off and idle him from it bodily, he cuts off his heart and idles it from standing before the Lord, exalted is He. So the servant was commanded to seek refuge in God from him, so that his standing before his Lord may be sound for him, his heart may come alive and be illumined by what he reflects upon and understands from the speech of his master, which is the cause of his life, his bliss and his success. Satan is most eager to cut his heart off from the purpose of the recitation.

When God, glorified is He, knew the earnestness of the enemy, his determination against the servant, and the servant's inability to resist him, He commanded him to seek refuge in Him and to take refuge with Him in turning him away, so that he is spared the burden of fighting and opposing him through seeking refuge. It is as though it were said to him: You have no power against this enemy, so seek refuge in Me and seek My protection, and I will suffice you against him and protect you from him.

One day Shaykh al-Islam, may God sanctify his spirit, said to me: "If the sheep's dog snaps at you, do not occupy yourself with fighting and repelling it; rather go to the shepherd and call for his help, for he will turn the dog away from you."

When he seeks refuge in God from Satan, Satan keeps far from him. The heart then turns to the meanings of the Qur'an, enters its pleasant gardens, witnesses its wonders which dazzle the intellects, and extracts from its treasures and stores what no eye has seen, no ear has heard. Between him and that stood the soul and Satan. The soul is receptive to Satan and listens to him. When he keeps away from it and is driven off, the angel draws near to it, strengthens it and reminds it of what contains its happiness and salvation.

When he begins reciting the Qur'an, he has stood in the station of addressing his Lord and conversing with Him. So let him take the utmost care to avoid provoking His hatred and wrath by conversing with Him and addressing Him while he is turned away from Him and turned towards other than Him, for by that he invites His hatred. He is like a man whom a king of the kings of this world has brought near and set before him, and who then begins to address the king while turning his back to him or turning his face away to the right and the left. What then is the thought of the king's hatred for this? What then is the thought of the True King, the Manifest, who is the Lord of the worlds, the Sustainer of the heavens and the earth?

And let him stop at every verse of the Fatihah, awaiting his Lord's answer to him, as though he heard Him say: My servant praised Me when he says: ﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾. When he says: ﴿The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾, he pauses a moment awaiting His saying: My servant has extolled Me. When he says: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾, he awaits His saying: My servant has glorified Me. When he says: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾, he awaits His saying: This is between Me and My servant. When he says: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ to the end, he awaits His saying: These are for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asked.

Whoever has tasted the flavour of prayer knows that nothing else can take the place of the takbir and the Fatihah, just as nothing else can take the place of standing, bowing and prostration in it. Each act of servitude in prayer has a secret, an effect and a servitude that cannot be obtained from anything else. Then each verse of the Fatihah has a servitude, a taste and an ecstasy specific to it.

[Section: The name (Allah) indicates the attribute by itself and indicates the pure Essence.]

**Second principle:** Among the names of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, each name indicates the Essence and the attribute from which it is derived by direct indication (muṭābaqa). It also indicates two further kinds of indication: by inclusion (taḍammun) and by necessary implication (luzūm). So it indicates the attribute alone by inclusion, and likewise the Essence stripped of the attribute. It also indicates another attribute by necessary implication. For example, the name al-Samī' (the All-Hearing) indicates the Lord's Essence and His hearing by direct indication, the Essence alone and hearing alone by inclusion, and the name al-Ḥayy (the Ever-Living) and the attribute of life by necessary implication. The same applies to all His names and attributes. However, people differ in knowing whether a necessary implication exists. From this arises much of their disagreement concerning the names, attributes and rulings. Whoever knows that voluntary action is necessarily linked to life, that hearing and sight are necessarily linked to complete life, and that all other perfection follows necessarily from complete life, will affirm from the names, attributes and acts of the Lord what those who do not know this necessary link will deny. Such people do not know the reality of life or its necessary implications. The same applies to His other attributes.

The name al-ʿAẓīm (the Mighty) has necessary implications which whoever does not know the greatness of Allah and its implications will deny.

Likewise the name al-ʿAlī (the Most High), the name al-Ḥakīm (the All-Wise) and His other names. From the necessary implications of al-ʿAlī is absolute highness in every respect. He has absolute highness from all aspects: highness of rank, highness of dominion, and highness of Essence. Whoever denies the highness of His Essence has denied the necessary implications of His name al-ʿAlī.

Likewise His name al-Ẓāhir (the Manifest) has as one of its implications that nothing is above Him, as in the authentic report from the Prophet (ﷺ): "You are al-Ẓāhir, so there is nothing above You." Rather, He, glory be to Him, is above everything. Whoever denies His being above (fawqiyya) has denied the necessary implications of His name al-Ẓāhir. It is not valid that al-Ẓāhir means only the one who has superiority of rank, as one says: "Gold is above silver," or "The gem is above glass." That superiority relates to manifestness, and sometimes the one who is surpassed is more manifest in that respect than the one who surpasses. Nor is it valid that manifestness means only manifestness of dominion and victory, although He, glory be to Him, is manifest by dominion and victory. The name is set in contrast with al-Bāṭin (the Hidden), who is such that nothing is beneath Him, just as the first (al-Awwal, the First) is contrasted with al-Ākhir (the Last), who has nothing after Him.

Likewise, the name al-Ḥakīm (the All-Wise) has as its implications the establishment of praiseworthy and intended ends through His acts, His placing things in their proper places, and His bringing them about in the best manner. Denying this is a denial of this name and its implications. The same applies to all His Beautiful Names.

**[Chapter: The name (Allāh) indicates the Beautiful Names]**

Once these two principles are established, the name Allah indicates all the Beautiful Names and the Lofty Attributes by the three kinds of indication. It indicates His divinity (ilāhiyya), which includes the affirmation of the attributes of divinity for Him together with the negation of their opposites.

The attributes of divinity are the attributes of perfection, free from resemblance and likeness, and from defects and deficiencies. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, attributes all the Beautiful Names to this Mighty Name, as in His saying: ﴿And to Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names﴾ [al-A'raf: 180]. One says: "ar-Raḥmān, ar-Raḥīm, al-Quddūs, as-Salām, al-ʿAzīz and al-Ḥakīm are among the names of Allah." But one does not say: "Allah is among the names of ar-Raḥmān, or among the names of al-ʿAzīz," and similar.

It is therefore known that the name Allah necessarily includes all the meanings of the Beautiful Names and indicates them in summary. The Beautiful Names are a detailed explanation and clarification of the attributes of divinity from which the name Allah is derived. The name Allah indicates that He is the One worshipped and served (maʾlūh, maʿbūd), whom creation worships out of love, veneration, humility, and turning to Him in needs and calamities. This necessarily implies the perfection of His lordship (rubūbiyya) and His mercy, and these two include the perfection of sovereignty (mulk) and praise (ḥamd). His divinity, His lordship, His mercy and His sovereignty necessarily imply all the attributes of His perfection, since it is impossible for these to be established for one who is not living, not hearing, not seeing, not powerful, not speaking, not doing what He wills, and not wise in His acts.

The attributes of majesty and beauty (jalāl and jamāl) are especially proper to the name Allah.

The attributes of action, power, sole authority over harm and benefit, giving and withholding, the effectiveness of will, perfection of strength, and management of the affairs of creation are especially proper to the name al-Rabb (the Lord).

The attributes of benevolence, generosity and kindness, tenderness and bounty, compassion and gentleness are especially proper to the name ar-Raḥmān (the Most Merciful). It was repeated to announce the establishment of the attribute, the occurrence of its effect, and its connection to what it affects.

So ar-Raḥmān is the one whose attribute is mercy, and ar-Raḥīm is the one who shows mercy to His servants. For this reason Allah says: ﴿And He is ever Merciful to the believers﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 43], and ﴿Indeed He is, to them, Kind and Merciful﴾ [al-Tawba: 117]. It has not come as "Raḥmān to His servants," or "Raḥmān to the believers," together with what is in the name ar-Raḥmān, which is on the pattern faʿlān, indicating the breadth of this attribute and the establishment of its whole meaning in the one described by it.

Do you not see that they say: ghaḍbān (full of anger) for one filled with anger, nadmān (full of regret), ḥayrān (bewildered), sakrān (intoxicated) and lahfān (longing) for one filled with that? So the pattern faʿlān is for breadth and comprehensiveness. For this reason Allah frequently links His istiwāʾ (being established) over the Throne with this name, as in His saying: ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 5], and ﴿Then the Most Merciful established Himself upon the Throne﴾ [al-Furqān: 59]. He established Himself upon His Throne with the name ar-Raḥmān, because the Throne encompasses the created beings and embraces them, and mercy encompasses creation and is broad toward them. As Allah says: ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 156]. He established Himself over the greatest of created things with the most encompassing of attributes, and therefore His mercy encompasses all things.

In the Ṣaḥīḥ, from the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah had decreed creation, He wrote in a Book which is with Him, placed upon the Throne: Indeed My mercy overcomes My wrath." In another wording: "It is with Him upon the Throne."

Reflect on the particularity of this Book with mention of mercy, and its placement with Him upon the Throne. Connect that with His saying: ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 5] and His saying: ﴿Then the Most Merciful established Himself upon the Throne; so ask about Him one who is informed﴾ [al-Furqān: 59]. A great door of knowledge of the Lord, blessed and exalted, will open for you, unless denial (taʿṭīl) and tajahhum (the Jahmite denial of divine attributes) close it to you.

The attributes of justice, of constriction and expansion, of lowering and raising, of giving and withholding, of granting honour and humiliation, of subjugation and judgement, and the like, are especially proper to the name al-Malik (the King). He specified it with the Day of Religion (Yawm al-Dīn), which is the day of recompense with justice, because He alone is sole judge on that day, and because it is the true day, and what precedes it is like an hour, and because it is the final end, while the days of this world are stages leading to it.

**(A subtle point)**

Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

I have seen that Ibn Fūrak has something close to this concerning the name (Allāh). He said: The wisdom in the presence of the alif at its beginning is that it is from the furthest point of exit of the voice, near the heart, which is the seat of knowledge, toward which [the voice moves]. Then the hāʾ at its end has its exit from the same place as well, because the beginning comes from it and the return is to it, and repetition is easier than initiation. Likewise the sound of the hāʾ is easier than the sound of the hamza. This is the meaning of his words.

Those in the grammarians' tradition did not say what we have said about pronouns except by drawing on the principles of the leading grammarians and by inference from the rules of the language. So reflect on these secrets. Let not the dullness of the nature of most people concerning them, nor their contentment with the outward of the worldly life, keep you away from them, nor from thinking about them and attending to them. I have only examined these secrets and the hidden reasons in outward forms and pronouns, seeking to reflect and take lesson concerning the wisdom of Him who ﴿created man, taught him speech﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 3–4].

So whenever some of these secrets shine for you, and their hidden treasures are revealed to you through reflection, thank the Giver of the blessing: ﴿Say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 114].

**[Benefit: On the name, the named, and the naming]**

The word composed of the letters zāy, yāʾ and dāl, for example, has a distinct and established reality, so it deserves to have a word assigned to it that indicates it, because it is a thing existing in speech and heard by ears. The word composed of the hamzat al-waṣl, sīn and mīm is an expression of the word composed of zāy, yāʾ and dāl, for example. The word composed of zāy, yāʾ and dāl is an expression of the person existing in reality and in minds, and that is the named (musammā). The word indicating it, which is zāy, yāʾ and dāl, is the name (ism). And this word itself has also become a named thing, from the viewpoint that the word hamza, sīn and mīm is an expression of it. So it is clear to you that the name, in its original assignment, is not the named. Therefore you say: "I named this person with this name," just as you say: "I adorned him with this adornment," and the adornment is other than the one adorned. Likewise the name is other than the named. Sībawayh stated this explicitly, and whoever attributed to him otherwise and claimed that his doctrine is the identity of the two has erred. What deceived those who made that claim is his saying that verbs are patterns taken from the forms of nouns. But this does not contradict his earlier explicit statement, for he stated that the name is other than the named. He said: "Name, verb and particle." So he explicitly stated that the name is a word. How can the word be the named, when the named is a person? Then he said after this: "You say: I named Zayd with this name, just as you say: I marked him with this sign." And in his book, in nearly a thousand places, he says that the name is the word indicating the named. Whenever the genitive case, the accusative, the tanwīn, the definite article, or everything that attaches to the name of addition, subtraction, diminutive, broken plural, declension or indeclinability is mentioned, all of that is an accident of the name, and nothing of it has any connection at all to the named. Is the name the same as the named?

No grammarian or Arab has ever said that the name is the named. They say "the named (musammā)," and they say "yes, the named," but they do not say "yes, the name." They say "the named of this name is so-and-so," and no one says "the name of this name is so-and-so." They say "this man is named Zayd (musammā bi-Zayd)," and they do not say "this man is the name of Zayd." They say "bismillāh" and do not say "bi-musammā Allāh." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have five names," reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim, and it is not valid to say: "I have five named things." And "Name yourselves with my name," reported by Muslim, and it is not valid to say: "Name yourselves with my named things." And "Allah has ninety-nine names," reported by al-Bukhārī, Muslim and Aḥmad, and it is not valid to say: "ninety-nine named things."

When the difference between the name and the named has become clear, there remains here the act of naming (tasmiya). It is what those who hold that the name and the named are identical have considered. Naming is the act of the one who names, and his assigning the name to the named, just as adorning (taḥliya) is the act of the one who adorns, and his placing the adornment upon the adorned. So here there are three realities: name, named and naming, like adornment, adorned and adorning, and sign, signified and signifying (ʿalāma, muʿallam, taʿlīm). It is impossible to make two of them synonyms with one meaning, because their realities differ. If you make the name the named, one of these three realities disappears, without doubt.

If it is said: "Then tell us the basis of those who hold that the two are identical, so that the proof is complete, for you have established your proof, and you must answer the objection." Among their arguments is that Allah alone is the Creator, and whatever else is created. So if His names were other than Him, they would be created. And it would follow that He had no name in eternity, nor attribute, because His names are attributes. This is the great question which led the affirmers of attributes (mutakallimūn al-ithbāt) to say that the name is the named. So what do you have to answer it?

The answer is that the source of error in this matter lies in using general terms that are ambiguous, admitting two meanings, one sound and one false. The dispute cannot be settled except by distinguishing those meanings and applying the terms to them. There is no doubt that Allah, blessed and exalted, has never ceased and does not cease to be described by the attributes of perfection, from which His names are derived. He has always been with His names and attributes, and He is one God, to whom belong the Beautiful Names and the Lofty Attributes. His names and attributes are included in the named by His name, although the attribute is not called "God who creates and provides." Therefore His attributes and names are not other than Him, and they are not the very essence of God. The trouble of the people lies in the word "other (ghayr)," for it is used with two meanings. One is that which is distinct from that Essence named Allah. Everything that is distinct from Allah in pure distinction, in this sense, is created. The other meaning is the distinction of the attribute from the Essence when it is taken apart from it. So if one says: "The knowledge of Allah and the speech of Allah are other than Him," in the sense that they are other than the bare Essence stripped of knowledge and speech, the meaning is sound, but the unqualified expression is false. And if it is meant that knowledge and speech are distinct from His particular reality, by which He is distinguished from others, then it is false both in wording and in meaning.

On this basis the People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna) answered the Muʿtazila (Muʿtazila, the rationalist school), who held that the Qur'an is created. They said: His speech, exalted is He, is included in the named by His name. Allah is the name of the Essence described by the attributes of perfection, and among these attributes is the attribute of speech, just as His knowledge, power, life, hearing and sight are uncreated. Since the Qur'an is His speech and is one of His attributes, it includes His Beautiful Names. If the Qur'an is uncreated and it cannot be said that it is other than Allah, how can it be said that part of what it includes, namely His names, is created and other than Him? Thus, praise be to Allah, the truth has become clear and the difficulty has been resolved. His Beautiful Names that are in the Qur'an are part of His speech, and His speech is uncreated. It cannot be said that it is other than Him, nor that it is He. This position differs from that of the Muʿtazila, who say His names are other than Him and created, and also from that of those who refute them by saying His name is the very essence of His Self and not other than it. With detailed analysis, doubts disappear and the correct view becomes evident, and praise belongs to Allah.

A second argument they raise: Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 78], ﴿And mention the name of your Lord﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 8], and ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Aʿlā: 1]. This argument is in reality against them, because the Prophet (ﷺ) carried out this command and said: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High," "Glory be to my Lord, the Mighty." If the matter were as they claim, he would have said: "Glory be to the name of my Lord, the Mighty." Moreover, the whole community does not permit anyone to say: "I worshipped the name of my Lord," or "I prostrated to the name of my Lord," or "I bowed to the name of my Lord," or "by the name of my Lord, have mercy on me." This indicates that acts are connected to the named, not to the name.

As for the answer concerning the connection of remembrance and glorification commanded with the name, it has been said that when glorification and exaltation are due to the one exalted, then what is of his cause and connected to him is also exalted, as one says: "Peace be upon the lofty gate, the noble assembly," and similar. But this answer is not satisfactory for two reasons. The first is that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not understand this meaning, but said: "Glory be to my Lord," and he did not turn to what you have mentioned.

The second argument: it would follow that the name can be applied to takbir, tahmid, tahlil and all else that is applied to the named, so one would say "al-hamdu li-ism Allah" and "la ilaha illa ism Allah" and the like. No one has said this. Rather, the correct answer is that true remembrance (dhikr haqiqi) has its locus in the heart, because it is the opposite of forgetfulness, and glorification (tasbih) is a kind of dhikr. So if dhikr and tasbih were applied without qualification, what would be understood from them would be only that, not verbal utterance with the tongue. God, exalted is He, desired both from His servants together, and He did not accept faith and the bond of Islam except with the conjunction and union of the two. So the meaning of the two verses becomes: glorify your Lord with your heart and your tongue, and remember your Lord with your heart and your tongue. The word "ism" is therefore inserted to point to this meaning, so that glorification and remembrance are not devoid of utterance with the tongue. For the remembrance of the heart has as its object the named (al-musamma), indicated by the name and not anything else, whereas remembrance with the tongue has as its object the utterance together with what it signifies, since the utterance is not intended for itself. So no one imagines that the utterance itself is what is glorified, apart from the meaning it indicates. My shaykh, Abu al-Abbas Ibn Taymiyya, may God sanctify his spirit, expressed this meaning to me in a subtle and concise phrase: "The meaning is: glorify, speaking the name of your Lord," i.e. uttering it. Similarly: ﴿What you worship besides Him are only names you have named﴾ and ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord﴾, the meaning being: glorify your Lord mentioning His name. This benefit is worth a journey, but only to one who knows its worth. So praise be to God, the Bestower, by His grace, and we ask Him for the completion of His favour.

The third argument: they said, God, exalted is He, said: ﴿What you worship besides Him are only names you have named﴾, and they only worshipped what the names designate. The answer: as you have said, they only worshipped the named things, but because they had given them false names, such as al-Lat and al-Uzza, which are mere false names with no real named referent. They named them gods and worshipped them because they believed in the real divinity of these, whereas they had no divinity except the bare names, not the reality of the named. So they worshipped only names with no realities corresponding to them. This is like one who names onion skins "meat" and eats them: it is said, "You ate nothing of the meat but its name, not its reality." Or like one who names dust "bread" and eats it: it is said, "You ate only the name of bread." Indeed, this negation is more emphatic regarding their gods, for there is no reality of divinity for them in any respect, and no wisdom in them beyond a mere name. So reflect on this noble benefit in His words, exalted is He.

If it is asked: what is the purpose of the particle "bi" (with) in His words ﴿So glorify with the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾, while it is not present in His words ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾?

It is answered: tasbih is intended to mean declaring God free of imperfection, which is bare remembrance with no further meaning, and it is also intended to mean that together with prayer, which is remembrance and declaration of freedom from imperfection together with action; this is why prayer is called tasbih. When bare tasbih is intended, there is no sense in "bi", because it is not transitive with a prepositional particle: you do not say "sabbahtu bi-Allah". When you intend what is joined with action, which is prayer, you add "bi" to point to that intended meaning, as if you said: "glorify, beginning with the name of your Lord" or "uttering the name of your Lord", just as you say "pray, beginning with it" or "uttering His name". For this reason, God knows best, the lam appears in His words ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies God (sabbaha lillah)﴾, and the intended tasbih is that which is prostration, submission and obedience. He did not say in any place "sabbaha Allah ma fi al-samawat wa al-ard", as He said ﴿And to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾.

Reflect on His words, exalted is He: ﴿Those who are with your Lord do not disdain His worship, and they glorify Him, and to Him they prostrate﴾. How He said ﴿and they glorify Him﴾ when He mentioned prostration by its specific name: so tasbih becomes their mention of Him and their declaring Him free of imperfection.

The fourth argument: they said the poet said:
"Until the year is complete, then the name of peace upon you both, and whoever weeps a full year has made an excuse."
And likewise the words of al-A'sha:
"A caller calls to it by the name of water, a tawny (gazelle)."

This is an argument against them, not for them. As for his words "then the name of peace upon you both", "peace" is God, exalted is He, and "peace" also means greeting. If he means the first, there is no difficulty: it is as if he said "then the name of Peace upon you both", i.e., the blessing of His name. If he means greeting, then "peace" denotes the signified meaning, and "name" the utterance that indicates it, so the meaning is: then the name of this named thing upon you both. The first refers to the utterance and the second to the meaning, as you say: "Zayd is a duck" and the like, where one of the two terms is meant as the word and the other as what it signifies. There is a fine subtlety in it: as if he meant, "then this utterance remains upon you both, continuing, not cut off from me; rather I am observing it constantly." Abu Suhayl al-Suhayli answered the verse with another answer, and this is a quotation of his words. He said: Labid did not intend to convey the greeting to them at that moment; he meant after the year. Had he said "peace upon you both", it would have been a greeting at the moment of his utterance of the verse. Likewise the mention of the name, which is an expression for the utterance, means that the utterance of greeting is after the year. This is because greeting is a supplication, which is not restricted to a future time; it is for its moment. Do you not see that one does not say "after Friday, O God, have mercy on Zayd", nor "after death, O God, forgive me"? One says "O God, forgive me after death", so that "after" is an adverb of the forgiveness, while the supplication occurs at its moment. If you want to make the time an adverb of the supplication, you must state the verb, saying "after Friday I supplicate with such-and-such" or "I greet" or "I utter such-and-such", because adverbs are intended to denote events occurring in them, whether reports, commands or prohibitions. As for other meanings such as divorce, oath, supplication, wishing and questioning, they occur at the moment of their utterance. Likewise divorce occurs from one who says "after Friday you are divorced", and he is divorced at that moment. If he says "after the year, by God, I shall go out", the oath takes effect immediately, and it does not help him to say "I meant not to swear except after the year", for had he meant that he would have said "after the year I swear" or "after Friday I divorce you". As for command, prohibition and report, they are restricted by adverbs because adverbs in reality apply to the action commanded and reported, not to the command or report itself, since those occur at the moment of utterance. So when you say "hit Zayd on Friday", it is the hitting that is restricted to Friday, while as for the command, you are commanding it now. Likewise when you say "Zayd travelled on Friday", what is restricted to the day is the thing reported, not the report. Just as in "hit him on Friday", what is restricted by the adverb is the commanded action, not your command. So the adverb relates only to events, and the whole matter returns to a single principle. Had Labid said "until the year, then peace upon you both", it would have been a greeting at its moment; but he meant not to utter the greeting and farewell except after the year, and likewise the mention of the name, which has the meaning of the utterance of greeting, so that what comes after the year is its adverb. This answer is among his wonders and marvels, may God have mercy on him.

As for his words "a caller calls to it by the name of water": the water here, which is well known, is the drinkable reality, and for this reason he defined it as the mental reality. The verse is by Dhu al-Rumma, and its first half is:
"The eye is not refreshed except by what it looks upon."
Then he said: "A caller calls to it by the name of water." The careless interpreter thought that he meant to imitate the cry of the gazelle, and that she called her young with this sound, which is "mama". This is not his meaning. The poet is speaking in riddles: since there occurred a coincidence between the word for drinkable water and her cry with it, her cry became as if it were the word expressing drinkable water, so it is as if she cries out by the name of this drinkable water. This is because her cry is "mama", and this is most clear.

[Benefit: the name "Allah" and derivation]
Abu al-Qasim al-Suhayli and his shaykh Ibn al-Arabi claimed that the name Allah is not derived, because derivation requires a root from which it is derived, while His name, exalted is He, is eternal, and the eternal has no root, so derivation is impossible. There is no doubt that if derivation is meant in this sense, namely that it is drawn from another origin, then it is false. But those who held derivation did not mean this sense, nor did it cross their hearts. They meant only that it indicates an attribute of His, exalted is He, which is divinity, like all His beautiful names, such as the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, the Forgiving, the Merciful, the All-Hearing and the All-Seeing. These names are indisputably derived from their verbal nouns, and they are eternal, and the eternal has no root. Whatever your answer is regarding these names is the answer of those who hold that the name Allah is derived. Then the answer to all of them is that by derivation we mean only that they correspond to their sources in utterance and meaning, not that they are generated from them as a branch from its root. The grammarians' calling the verbal noun the root and the derived word the branch does not mean that one was generated from the other. Rather, the Arabs spoke with nouns first and then derived verbs from them; but communication by verbs is as necessary as communication by nouns, and there is no difference between them. So derivation here is not material derivation, but a derivation of mutual implication, called "the implying derived from the implied", since one of them implies the other and more. Sibawayh's saying that the verb is patterns taken from the form of the nominal events is in this sense, not that the Arabs spoke with nouns first and then derived verbs from them. For communication by verbs is necessary, as communication by nouns is, and there is no difference between them. So derivation here is not material derivation, but derivation of mutual implication, in which the implying (with kasra) is called derived and the implied (with fatha) is called that from which it is derived, and there is no objection to deriving the names of God, exalted is He, in this sense.

[Benefit: is "al-Rahman" in the basmala an adjective?]
Some people found it unlikely that al-Rahman is an adjective (na't) of God, from our saying ﴿In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾, and they said: al-Rahman is a proper name, and proper names are not used as adjectives. Then they said: it is an apposition (badal) from the name Allah. They said: what supports this is that al-Rahman is a proper name specific to God, exalted is He, in which no other shares, so it is unlike the attributes such as the Knowing, the Powerful, the Hearing and the Seeing, which are applied to others as well. They also said that what supports it is its occurrence in the Qur'an not following what precedes it, as in His words ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ and ﴿The Most Merciful taught the Qur'an﴾, and ﴿Who is this who is an army for you to help you, other than the Most Merciful?﴾; and this is the characteristic of pure names, since attributes are not confined to mention without the described. Al-Suhayli said: In my view, apposition is impossible here, and likewise explanatory apposition (atf al-bayan), because the first name needs no explanation, being the most definite of all definites and the clearest. For this reason they said "What is al-Rahman?" and did not say "What is Allah?" But although it follows the pattern of proper names, it is a descriptive term intended for praise. The same applies to al-Rahim, except that al-Rahman is of the intensive patterns, like ghadban and the like. The sense of intensity entered it because it has an alif and nun at its end, as in the dual, since the dual is in reality doubling. This descriptive pattern is likewise: ghadban and sakran are complete with two doublings of anger and intoxication. So the form resembles the dual, since the dual is in reality two. You see that they also likened the dual to this pattern when two mutually connected things are meant, saying "al-hakamān" and "al-ʿalamān", and they made the nun inflected as if it were the name of one thing. They said the pattern fa'lan and the dual pattern share this feature. From it is the saying of Fatima: "O Hasanan, O Husaynan", with the nun raised for her two sons. Because of its resemblance to the dual, its plural was prevented, so one does not say "ghadabin", and its feminine was prevented, so one does not say "ghadbana"; and its nunation was prevented, as the nun of the dual is not nunated. So many rulings of the dual apply to it, because it resembles it in form and meaning.

The benefit of combining the two attributes (al-Rahman and al-Rahim) is to inform of a mercy that is immediate and deferred, specific and general. End of his words.

I say: the names of the Lord, exalted is He, are both names and attributes, for they indicate the attributes of His perfection, so there is no contradiction between being a proper name and being a descriptive term. Al-Rahman is His name and His attribute, and its being a name does not exclude its being a descriptor. Insofar as it is a descriptor, it follows the name Allah; insofar as it is a name, it occurs in the Qur'an not as a follower, just as a proper name occurs. Since this name is specific to Him, exalted is He, it is fitting for it to come alone without following, as the name Allah comes so. This does not contradict its indication of the attribute of mercy, just as the name Allah, exalted is He, indicates the attribute of divinity, yet never came as a follower of another, but always as the one followed. This is unlike the Knowing, the Powerful, the Hearing, the Seeing and the like, which do not come alone but as followers. Reflect on this marvellous subtlety, and it will become clear to you that al-Rahman is a name and an attribute, neither of which excludes the other, and the Qur'an's usage has come with both together. As for combining al-Rahman with al-Rahim, it contains a meaning better than the two meanings he mentioned: al-Rahman indicates the attribute subsisting in Him, glorified is He, and al-Rahim indicates its connection to the one shown mercy. So the first is for the description and the second for the act. The first indicates that mercy is His attribute, and the second indicates that He shows mercy to His creatures by His mercy. If you wish to understand this, reflect on His words ﴿And He is ever merciful to the believers﴾ and ﴿Indeed He is to them Kind and Merciful﴾; and "Rahman" never came with "bihim". It is thus known that al-Rahman is the one described with mercy, and al-Rahim is the one who shows mercy by His mercy. This is a subtlety you will hardly find in a book, and if the mirror of your heart breathes upon it, its form will not be clear to you.

[Benefit: omission of the governing verb in "bismillah"]
Omitting the governing verb in "bismillah" has many benefits. Among them: it is a position in which nothing should precede except the mention of God. Had you mentioned the verb, which cannot do without its agent, that would contradict the purpose; so omitting it makes the wording match the meaning, so that what begins with it is the name of God, as we say in prayer "Allahu akbar", whose meaning is "from everything", but we do not say this supposed thing. And so that the wording corresponds to the intention of the heart, which is that nothing be in the heart except God alone: just as His mention is bare in the heart of the worshipper, so it is bare on his tongue. Another: when the verb is omitted, it is correct to begin with the basmala in every act, speech and movement, and no verb has priority over another for it, so omission is more general than mention, for whatever verb you mention, the omitted one is more general than it. Another: omission is more emphatic, for the speaker of this phrase seems to claim that he is sufficient by the witnessing of the situation without uttering the verb, as if there were no need to utter it, since the situation and the context indicate that this and every act is by His name, blessed and exalted. Referring to the witness of the situation is more emphatic than referring to the witness of speech, as it is said:
"And it is strange, the reproach of the blamers regarding one who is in love; and is there anything but the one I love who is loved and adored?"

[Benefit: connecting the prayer upon the Prophet to the basmala]
Some people found it problematic that the authors say "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" and then "and may God bless Muhammad and his family", and they said: the verb after the conjunction is a supplication for blessing, while the basmala before it is an informative statement, and a supplication should not be conjoined to an informative statement. If you say "I passed by Zayd and may God forgive you", it would be poor speech. The basmala is in the sense of a statement, because the meaning is "do such-and-such in the name of God." The one who affirmed it argued by following the predecessors.

The answer to what they said is that the conjunction did not join a supplication to a statement; rather, the clause was joined to a quoted utterance, as if you said: "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" and "and may God bless Muhammad", or "I say this and this", or "I write this and this."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 1, verse 2 (part 1 of 14):

In his words ﴿Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, you find beneath this phrase the affirmation of every perfection of the Lord, exalted is He, in His acts, His attributes and His names, and His transcendence above every flaw and defect in His acts, His attributes and His names. He is praiseworthy in His acts, attributes and names, and free of faults and deficiencies in His acts, attributes and names. All His acts are wisdom, mercy, benefit and justice, and do not depart from this. All His attributes are attributes of perfection and descriptions of majesty, and all His names are the most beautiful. His praise fills this world, the Hereafter, the heavens and the earth, and what is between them and what is in them. The whole of existence speaks His praise. Creation and command proceed from His praise, subsist by His praise, and came into being by His praise. So His praise is the cause of the existence of every existent, and it is the ultimate end of every existent. Every existent bears witness to His praise. His sending of His Messenger is by His praise, and His sending down of His books is by His praise. The Garden is populated with its people by His praise, and the Fire is populated with its people by His praise. He is obeyed only by His praise, and He is disobeyed only by His praise. Not a leaf falls except by His praise, and not an atom moves in existence except by His praise.

He is praiseworthy in Himself, even if the servants do not praise Him, just as He is the One, the Unique, even if the servants do not affirm His oneness, and the true God even if they do not worship Him. He, glorified is He, is the One who praised Himself upon the tongue of the speaker: "Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah, the Exalted, said upon the tongue of His Prophet: Allah hears the one who praises Him."

So He is, in reality, the one who praises Himself upon the tongue of His servant, for He is the One who makes praise flow upon his tongue and in his heart. His making it flow is by His praise. To Him belongs all praise, to Him belongs all dominion, in His hand is all good, and to Him all affairs return. This knowledge is part of the servitude of praise.

Also among His servitude is that the servant knows that his praise of his Lord, exalted is He, is itself a blessing from Him upon him, for which he deserves praise. If he praises Him for this blessing, that makes him deserving of another praise for the blessing of praising Him, and so on without end. Even if the servant spent all his breaths in praising Him for one of His blessings, what is due to Him of praise and what He deserves would still exceed that many times over, and no one can ever count the praise due to Him for His praiseworthy qualities.

Also among the servant's servitude is his witnessing of his own inability to praise, and that whatever praise he does perform, the Lord, exalted is He, is the one who is praised for it, since He is the One who causes it to flow upon his tongue and in his heart.

Also among his servitude is that he applies praise to all the details of his circumstances, outward and inward, whether they are what he loves or what he dislikes. He, exalted is He, is in reality the one praised for all of that, even if it is absent from the servant's witnessing.

Then, in His words ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, there is in the servitude the witnessing of His singular lordship, exalted is He, and that just as He is the Lord of the worlds, their Creator, their Provider, the Manager of their affairs, the One who brings them into existence and the One who annihilates them, so He alone is their God, their object of worship, their refuge and their recourse in calamities. There is no lord other than Him, and no god besides Him.

(A subtle point)
Ja'far ibn Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with him, said: My father lost a mule of his, and he said: "If Allah returns it to me, I will praise Him with praises that He is pleased with." Not long after, its saddle and bridle were brought to him, and he mounted it. When he was settled on it and gathered his garments to himself, he raised his head to the sky and said: "Praise belongs to Allah," and he added nothing to it.
He was asked about that, and he said: "Did I leave anything out or keep anything back?" I have made all praise belong to Allah.

(The difference between hamd and madh)
The difference between them is that hamd (praise rooted in love and esteem) includes commendation together with knowledge of what is being commended. If it is stripped of knowledge, it is madh (mere praise) and not hamd. So every hamd is madh, but not every madh is hamd. And since hamd includes knowledge of the qualities of the one praised, its verb came in the form ḥamida with the vowel of ʿalima (to know), matching it, whereas madh did not come in that form. Thus madh is used for outward actions, like striking and the like. For this reason, in the Book and the Sunna, one says "Hamida Rabbanā falānan" (our Lord praised so-and-so) and "Yamdaḥu Allāhu falānan" (Allah praises so-and-so), and "athnā ʿalā falān" (he commended so-and-so), and one does not say "ḥamida" except of Himself. That is why He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Praise belongs to Allah﴾, with the definite article of the genus, which conveys totality. So all praise belongs to Him, either as dominion or as entitlement. His praise of Himself is entitlement, while the praise of the servants of Him, and the praise of some of them for others, is a dominion belonging to Him. If He praised someone else, it would not be proper to say that this praise belongs to Him as dominion, because praise is His speech, and it could not be attributed to Him as entitlement while it is directed toward another.

If it is said: Is not His commendation and praise of His friends only by what He knows, so why should it not be called hamd?
It is answered: Only that which includes knowledge of perfect excellences is called hamd without qualification, and that is absent in anyone other than Him, glorified is He. So when He praises someone, He praises him for a quality that is deficient with respect to the servant, and He knows its deficiency. When He praises Himself, He praises Himself for what He knows of the perfection of His attributes.

I say: The distinction that he mentioned between hamd and madh, based on the presence or absence of knowledge, is not correct. Each of them includes knowledge of what one praises another for. Whoever does not know the attributes of the one praised is not a praiser or a hamid. How then can his statement be valid, that if it is stripped of knowledge it is madh? Rather, if it is stripped of knowledge, it is speech without knowledge: if it agrees with reality it is true, and otherwise it is false. As for his statement, "For this reason, hamd of our Lord for someone did not come in the Book and the Sunna," it must be said: Where in them did the praise of Allah for someone come? Indeed, in the Sunna there is something more specific than hamd, namely thana' (commendation), which is the repetition of praiseworthy qualities, as in the statement of the Prophet ﷺ to the people of Quba: "What is this purification by which Allah has commended you?" (authentic). Since He commended them, and thana' is repeated hamd, what prevents Him from praising whichever of His servants He wills?

Then, the correct view regarding the naming of the Prophet ﷺ as Muhammad is that he is the one whom Allah praises, and His angels, and the believing servants.
As for the one who said: he is the one whom the people of the heavens and the earth praise, this does not contradict Allah's praise of him. Rather, the praise of the people of the heavens and the earth for him comes after Allah's praise of him. When Allah praised him, the people of the heavens and the earth praised him.
In sum, when hamd is a particular commendation of the one praised, it is not impossible for Allah, exalted is He, to praise whichever of His creatures He wills, just as He commends him. So the correct account of the difference between hamd and madh is this: informing about the excellences of another is either information stripped of love and will, or information joined with love and will for him. If it is the first, it is madh; if it is the second, it is hamd. So hamd is information about the excellences of the one praised together with love for him, reverence for him and esteem for him. For this reason, it is an information that includes an inshāʾ (performative act), unlike madh, which is pure information. When the speaker says "al-ḥamdu lillāh" or "Rabbanā laka al-ḥamd," his speech includes information about everything for which He is praised, expressed with a comprehensive, all-encompassing name that includes every individual instance of praise, both actual and potential. This entails affirming every perfection for which the Lord, exalted is He, is praised. That is why this expression is not fitting in this form except for one whose state is this, namely the Praiseworthy, the Glorious. Since this meaning accompanies hamd, its reality cannot be established except with it. So whoever explained it as contentment and love has explained it by part of its meaning. Rather, it is contentment, love, and accompaniment of praise. For this reason, and Allah knows best, its verb came in the pattern of natural dispositions and innate qualities, so it was said ḥamida, because it includes love, which is more fitting and more appropriate to natural dispositions and innate traits, like "fahima" (understood), "ḥadhira" (was wary) and "saqima" (was sick) and the like. This is unlike pure information stripped of that, which is madh, for it came on the pattern of faʿala, so they said madahahu, because its meaning is stripped of the meanings of innate dispositions and natural traits. So reflect upon this marvelous point, and reflect on the performative act that is established in your saying "Rabbanā laka al-ḥamd" and your saying "al-ḥamdu lillāh," how you find it beneath these words. That is why one does not say, in their place, "al-madh lillāh" (praise belongs to Allah as madh) or "Rabbanā laka al-madh." Its secret is what I have mentioned to you: information about the excellences of the one praised, information joined with love for him, will for him, reverence for him and esteem for him.

If you say: This contradicts your statement that it is not impossible for Allah, exalted is He, to praise whichever of His creatures He wills, for Allah, exalted is He, is not made great by anything, and nothing other than Him deserves reverence. How then does He revere any of His servants?
I say: Love is never separated from reverence and esteem for the beloved. But it is ascribed to each entity according to what the particular attributes of that entity require. So the servant's love for his Lord entails his reverence and esteem for Him. Likewise, love for the Messenger entails honoring him, supporting him and esteeming him. Likewise, love for parents, scholars and just rulers. As for the Lord's love for His servant, it entails His honoring His servant and His generosity toward him, His elevating his mention, and His placing reverence and awe for him in the hearts of His friends. This meaning is established in His love and His praise of His servant, whether or not it is named reverence and esteem. Do you not see that His love for His messengers required that He elevate their mention among the people of the heavens and the earth, and raise their remembrance above the remembrance of others? He is angry with whoever does not love them, honor them and esteem them, and He sends upon him various punishments in this world and the Hereafter, and He makes His honor in this world and the Hereafter belong to those who love them, support them and follow them. Do you not see how He commanded His servants and His friends with prayer upon Him, which is reverence and commendation of their seal and best, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him? Is this not reverence for them, honor for them, generosity toward them and dignity for them?

If it is said: The difference between hamd and madh has become clear, the meaning has been made evident and its face has shone forth. So what is the difference between them and between thana' (commendation) and majd (glory)? The difference between hamd and madh, and between thana' and majd?
It is answered: We have exceeded our limits in what we are concerned with, but we will mention the difference for the sake of completing the benefit. We will mention a comprehensive division of these four meanings: hamd, madh, thana' and majd. We say: Informing about the excellences of another has three considerations. One is consideration from the standpoint of what is reported. Another is consideration from the standpoint of the report about it. The third is consideration from the standpoint of the state of the one reporting. From the first consideration, the division arises into hamd and majd. For what is reported is either among the attributes of greatness, majesty, expansiveness and what follows from them, or among the attributes of beauty and beneficence and what follows from them. If it is the first, it is majd, and if it is the second, it is hamd. This is because the root m-j-d in their language revolves around the meaning of expansiveness and abundance. From it comes their saying "amjada al-dābba ʿalfan," meaning he gave the beast abundant fodder. From it also comes "majada al-rajulu," so he is "mājid" when his goodness and beneficence to people abound. The poet said:
"You are a generous, noble one, when the north wind blows at night."
From it also comes their saying about the gharb tree and the mirkh and ʿifār trees, "istamjada," meaning that the fire in them abounded.
From the consideration of the report itself, the division arises into thana' and hamd. For the report about excellences is either repeated or not. If it is repeated, it is thana'; if not repeated, it is hamd. This is because thana' is derived from al-thanī, which is bending and turning one thing over another, as in "thanaytu al-thawb" (I folded the garment), and from it comes al-tathniya in grammar, so the one commended (muthnā) is repeated, meaning the excellences of the one commended are mentioned again and again.
From the consideration of the state of the one reporting, the division arises into madh and hamd. For the one who reports the excellences of another either accompanies his report with love and reverence for him, or not. If love accompanies it, it is hamd; otherwise it is madh. So these divisions are established and distinguished. Then reflect on the application of His words, exalted is He, in what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ related from Him: when the servant says ﴿Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, Allah says: "My servant has praised Me." When he says ﴿the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾, He says: "My servant has commended Me, for he has repeated his praise." When he says ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾, He says: "My servant has glorified Me, for he has described Me with sovereignty, greatness and majesty."
Narrated by Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i.

So praise Allah for what He has brought to you of these secrets and benefits without effort. Your eye did not stay awake for them, your thought did not travel away from its homeland for them, and you did not strip yourself of your familiar things in obtaining them. Rather, they are brides of meanings that are unveiled to you and escorted to you. You have the pleasure of enjoying them, and their dowry is paid by others. The gain is yours, and the loss is theirs.

[Section: The difference between hamd and shukr]
People have disputed the difference between hamd and shukr (gratitude): which of them is higher and more excellent?
In the hadith: "Hamd is the head of shukr. Whoever does not praise Allah has not thanked Him."
The difference between them is that shukr is more general with respect to its kinds and causes, and more specific with respect to its objects. Hamd is more general with respect to its objects, and more specific with respect to its causes.
The meaning of this is that shukr is by the heart as humility and submission, by the tongue as commendation and acknowledgment, and by the limbs as obedience and compliance. Its object is blessings, not the essential attributes. So one does not say: "We thank Allah for His life, His hearing, His sight and His knowledge." He is the one praised for these. Just as He is praised for His beneficence and His justice, shukr is for beneficence and blessings.
So everything to which shukr is attached is attached to hamd, without the converse. And everything by which hamd occurs, shukr occurs by it, without the converse. For shukr occurs by the limbs, while hamd occurs by the heart and the tongue.

(A benefit)
When it is said, "All praise belongs to Allah," this has two meanings:
The first: He is praised for everything and with everything by which the perfectly praiseworthy is praised, even if some of His creation also praise Him, as His messengers, prophets and their followers praise Him. That is part of His praise, blessed and exalted is He. Rather, He is the one praised in the primary sense, and whatever praise they received, they received it only by His praise. So He is the praised one first and last, outwardly and inwardly. This is like His being knowing of everything, while He has taught some of His creatures knowledge they would not have had without His teaching. In the transmitted supplication: "O Allah, to You belongs all praise, to You belongs all dominion, in Your hand is all good, and to You all affairs return. I ask You for all good and I seek refuge in You from all evil." He, glorified is He, has dominion, and He has given some of His creatures a share of dominion. To Him belongs praise, and He has given others a share of praise as He wills. Just as the dominion of the created is within His dominion, so their praise is within His praise. So there is no praised one who is praised for anything, small or great, except that Allah is the one praised for it in essence and also by priority. When the one who praises says, "O Allah, to You belongs all praise," what is meant is: You are the one deserving of every praise, not merely the external praise.
The second meaning: "To You belongs all praise" means the complete and perfect praise. This is specific to Allah, mighty and majestic is He, and no one else shares in it. The truth is that to Him belongs praise in both senses together: He has the universality and perfection of praise, and this is among His particular attributes, glorified is He. So He is praised in every state and for everything, with the most perfect and greatest praise, just as He has complete and universal dominion. Nothing owns everything except Him, and complete perfect dominion belongs only to Him. The followers of the messengers, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them, affirm for Him perfect dominion and perfect praise. They say that He is the Creator of everything, its Lord and its King, and nothing at all is outside His creation, power and will. So to Him belongs all dominion.
The Qadariyya Majusiyya (those who deny divine decree, likened to Zoroastrians) exclude the acts of servants from His dominion. Thus they exclude the obediences of the prophets, the messengers, the angels and the righteous from His dominion, just as they exclude all the movements of angels, jinn and humans from His dominion.
The followers of the messengers make all of that included under His dominion and His power, and they affirm perfect praise as well: that He is praised for all of that and for everything He has created and will create, because of the wisdom and praiseworthy ends that He intends by the act.
As for those who deny wisdom and causes among those who affirm divine decree, they in reality do not affirm praise for Him, just as they do not affirm wisdom for Him. For praise is a necessary consequence of wisdom, and wisdom exists only with respect to one who does something for a purpose, intending by what he does the wisdom that arises from his act. As for one who does nothing for any purpose at all, wisdom cannot be conceived with respect to him.

(Section: On explaining that His praise, exalted is He, includes everything He brings into being)

The purpose is to show that His praise and wisdom, may He be exalted, encompass everything He brings about of beneficence, blessing, trial and affliction, and everything He decrees of obedience and disobedience. He, glory be to Him, is praised for all of it and is thanked, with both praise (hamd al-madh) and thankfulness (hamd al-shukr).

As for praise (hamd al-madh), He is praised for everything He has created, since He is the Lord of the worlds: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾.

As for thankfulness (hamd al-shukr), all of this is a blessing for the believer when it is accompanied by its due response of gratitude. A blessing that is met with thankfulness becomes a blessing indeed. A trial or affliction that is met with patience becomes a blessing. Obedience is among the greatest of His blessings. As for disobedience, when it is accompanied by its due response of repentance, seeking forgiveness, turning back to Him, humility and submission, it produces praiseworthy effects and sought-after outcomes that are themselves a blessing, even though its cause is something displeasing and hateful to the Lord, may He be exalted. He loves what results from it, namely repentance and seeking forgiveness. He, glory be to Him, is more delighted at the repentance of His servant than a man who has lost his mount in a desolate, deadly desert, a mount carrying his food and drink. He despairs of it and of living, so he lies down and sleeps, then wakes to find the mount standing with its reins caught on the root of a tree, and he goes and takes hold of it. Allah is more delighted at the repentance of a servant who turns to Him than this man is at his mount. This great joy, to which nothing is comparable, is more beloved to Him, glory be to Him, than its absence. It has causes and necessary concomitants that cannot be avoided. Whatever obedience would occur without it, though it is beloved to Him, this joy is far more beloved to Him, and its existence without its concomitant is impossible. So there is in His decreeing its causes and prerequisites a wisdom that is profound and a blessing that is abundant. This is with respect to the Lord, majestic is His majesty.

As for the servant, his perfect servitude and submission may depend on causes that cannot be realised without them. So the decree of a sin upon him, when it is followed by repentance, turning back, submission, humility, brokenness and constant dependence on Allah, is a blessing in terms of its outcome and what follows from it, even though, in terms of its form and self, it is a trial and test. The Lord, may He be exalted, is praised for both matters.

If the sin is followed by the effects beloved to the Lord, glory be to Him, namely repentance, humility, turning back and brokenness, then it is precisely the servant's benefit. What counts is the completeness of the end, not the deficiency of the beginning. If it is not followed by that, this can only come from the corruption of his soul, its wickedness, and its lack of readiness to dwell near its Lord among the pure, noble spirits in the highest assembly. It is known that this soul contains whatever evil and corruption it contains, so that evil must come out of it from potential into actuality, so that the fitting consequences follow for it, and so that it dwells with those fit for its company and joins the wicked spirits in the lowest place. When such souls are prepared for that, it is wise that the causes which lead them to what they are prepared for, and what nothing else suits, be drawn out of them. The Lord, may He be exalted, is praised for His bounty and His kindness towards those who deserve kindness and bounty and who are receptive to it, since not everyone is receptive to His blessing. His praise and wisdom require that He not place His bounty and treasures in a place that does not receive them.

Nothing remains except the question: what is the wisdom in creating these spirits that are not receptive to His blessing? The answer to this has already been given in full. The creation of opposites and contraries, and the bringing about of their effects, is required by His lordship, wisdom, knowledge and might. The decree of the absence of this would be a diminishing of the lordship. Furthermore, these events are a blessing in respect of the believer, for when they occur he is commanded to reject them with his heart, his hand and his tongue, or with his heart alone, and he is commanded to strive against their perpetrators according to his ability. From this rejection and striving there results for him benefits for his heart, soul and body, and benefits for his worldly life and his Hereafter, which he would not attain without them. The primary purpose is the completion of His blessing upon His friends, His messengers and His elect. So employing His enemies in what completes His blessing upon His friends is the utmost wisdom. Allowing the people of disbelief, wickedness and disobedience to act in this way leads to the perfection that comes to them through opposing these people, striving against them, rejecting their ways, loyalty and enmity for His sake, and giving up their souls, wealth and strength for Him.

Complete servitude is not attained except through sincere love. Love is sincere only when the lover expends what he possesses of wealth, status and strength in seeking the pleasure of the Beloved and drawing near to Him. If he gives up his soul for Him, this is the highest rank of love. It is known that among the necessary concomitants of this, without which it cannot be attained, are the creation of essences, causes, deeds, characters and natures that require opposition to those whom He loves and who seek His pleasure. At that point sincere love is distinguished from other kinds. Everyone loves ease, comfort, rest and pleasure, and loves whoever brings those to him and procures them for him. But the real matter lies beyond this: love of Him, glory be to Him, and love of what He loves, which is the thing most hateful to souls and most burdensome for them, the thing that does not suit them. When the causes of this arise, it becomes clear who loves Allah for His own sake and who loves what should be loved of those who love Him merely for the sake of His creatures: food, drink, marriage and status. If they are given these things they are pleased, and if they are denied them they are angry, reproach their Lord, sometimes complain about Him, and sometimes abandon His worship. Had it not been for the creation of opposites, and the empowering of His enemies and the testing of His friends by them, the pure servitude of His servants who are His servants would not have been drawn out. There would not have come about the servitude of loyalty for His sake, enmity for His sake, love for His sake, hatred for His sake, giving for His sake and withholding for His sake, nor the servitude of giving up souls in striving against His enemies and supporting Him, nor the servitude of separating from what the servant most needs when seeking His pleasure, nor the servitude of enduring, in His cause, what the servant's soul dislikes, though in doing so he would be censuring himself and seeking refuge in the very ones who wronged him, having committed a fault in separating from them and in following them. As for loyalty to the Truth against them, it is by the opposites and the causes that necessitate it that these effects are realised.

Furthermore, had it not been for the empowering of desire and anger, and their motives over the servant, he would not have attained the virtue of patience, nor the striving of the soul, nor restraining it from its portions and desires, out of love for Allah, preference for His pleasure, and seeking nearness and closeness to Him. Moreover, without this, this human existence would not be human but angelic. Allah, glory be to Him, created His creation in stages. He created the angels as intellects without desires, and without a nature that demands anything contrary to what is willed, from a luminous substance that does not necessitate any of the effects or blameworthy natures. He created the animals with desires but without intellects. He created the two weighty species, the jinn and humankind, and placed in them intellects, desires and differing natures, for differing effects according to their substances, forms and compositions. These are the people of trial and test, and they are the ones exposed to reward and punishment. Had He willed, glory be to Him, He could have made His creatures of one nature and one kind, without differentiation among them. But what He has done, glory be to Him, is pure wisdom, the requirement of lordship and the demand of divinity. Had all creation been one nature and one pattern, the atheist would have found a pretext and said: this is the requirement of nature. Had He been an agent by choice, His actions and their effects would have varied, and He would have done a thing and its opposite, a thing and its contrary. Likewise, were it not for the observation of these events that are witnessed, the atheist would also have found a pretext and said: if this world had a creator who chooses, events in it would be found according to His will and choice. As al-Hasan or another reported, the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) used to say: "Exalted is our Lord, the Eternal. Had this creation not changed, the doubter in Allah would have said: if this world had a creator, He would have made it happen: now it is night, then day comes; now it is day, then night comes; now it is clear, then clouds come; now it is cloudy, then clear comes," and similar talk. For this reason, He, glory be to Him, in His Book argues by events at times and by their variation at other times, since both this and that necessitate His lordship, power and choice, and the occurrence of beings in accordance with His will. Thus the variation of His actions and their effects is among the greatest proofs of His lordship, wisdom and knowledge.

For this reason He, glory be to Him, created the human species in four categories:
The first, neither from a male nor a female: this is the creation of their father and origin, Adam.
The second, from a male without a female: like the creation of their mother Eve from a rib of Adam's ribs, without a female bearing her or carrying her in a womb.
The third, from a female without a male: like the creation of the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary (ﷺ).
The fourth, the creation of the rest of the human species from a male and a female. All of this is to show His servants the perfection of His power, the sweep of His will and the perfection of His wisdom, and that the matter is not as His enemies, the deniers and disbelievers in Him, suppose: that it is a natural matter which has always been so and always will be, and that the species has no father or mother, and that there is only wombs that expel and earth that carries, and a nature that does what is seen and observed. These ignorant, misguided people did not know that nature is a power and a quality needing its substrate and in need of something that bears it. It is among the strongest indications of the existence of His command in its nature and creation. He placed it in bodies and put into it these wondrous secrets. So nature is a creature among His creatures, a possession among His possessions, and a servant subjugated to His command and submitting to His will. The signs of craftsmanship, the marks of creation and origination, and the evidences of poverty and need bear witness that it is created and made, that it does not create or act, and that it has no disposal over its own essence or self, let alone that beings are ascribed to it.

The point is that the diversity and variation of created things is a necessary part of wisdom, lordship and dominion, and it is also one of the requirements of praise. So to Him belongs praise for all of this, the most complete and perfect praise. His creatures are the requirements of His names and attributes. Every name and attribute has an effect that must manifest in it and that it necessitates. It is impossible to nullify the effects of His names and attributes, just as it is impossible to nullify His essence from them. These effects have connections and necessary consequences which cannot fail to exist, as has already been pointed out. Furthermore, the variety of the causes of praise is something desired by the Lord, may He be exalted, and beloved to Him. Just as the causes of praise vary, so praise varies with their variation and multiplies with their multiplication. It is known that He, glory be to Him, is praised for His retribution against the people of crime and evil, just as He is praised for His honouring of the people of justice and goodness. So He is praised for this and for that, along with what follows from it: His praise for His forbearance, pardon, forgiveness, His waiving of His rights, His overlooking of His creatures' wrongs by it, and His pardoning of many of the offences of His servants. He warns them with a little of His punishment and retribution for the much that He has pardoned. Had He hastened His punishment upon them and seized them according to His right, He would have brought them to their appointed term, and He would not have left upon its back a single creature. But His mercy has preceded His wrath, His pardon has preceded His retribution, and His forgiveness has preceded His punishment. So to Him belongs praise for His pardon and His retribution, for His justice and His kindness, and there is no way to nullify the causes of His praise or any part of them. Let the intelligent person consider this point with the fullest consideration, let him give it its due, and it will reveal to him great doors of the secrets of destiny, and will bring him down into meadows of lush pasture and gardens of beauty. Allah is the Granter of success, the Guide to what is right.

Furthermore, Allah, glory be to Him, has diversified the proofs that point to Him and that make His servants know Him, with the utmost variety. He has turned the signs and struck the parables, so as to establish His conclusive proof over them and to complete His abundant blessing upon them, so that after that no one has any argument against them before Him. Rather, the argument is all His, the blessing is all His, and the power is all His. He has established His proof against them. Had He willed, He would have made them equal in guidance, as He, exalted, said: ﴿So to Allah belongs the conclusive argument. Had He willed, He would have guided you all﴾ [al-An'am: 149]. So He informed that to Him belongs the conclusive argument, which reaches the core of the heart, mingles with the intellect and unites with it, so that the intellect cannot repel it or deny it. Then He informed that He, glory be to Him, is able to guide all His creatures, and had He willed that, He would have done it, owing to the perfection of His power and the sweep of His will.
