Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "The heads of blessings are three. The first is the blessing of Islam, without which His blessings are not complete. The second is the blessing of well-being, without which life is not sweet. The third is the blessing of wealth, without which living is not complete."

When Sa'id al-Jurayri returned from the pilgrimage, he began saying: "Allah blessed us on our journey with such and such," and then said: "Enumerating blessings is part of gratitude."

Wahb passed by a afflicted man who was blind, leprous, paralysed, naked, with white patches on his skin, and he was saying: "Praise be to Allah for His blessings." A man who was with Wahb said: "What blessing remains for you that you praise Allah for?" The afflicted man said: "Cast your eye upon the people of the city and look at the multitude of its people. Shall I not praise Allah that there is no one in it who knows me except myself?"

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "When Allah bestows a blessing upon a servant and he praises Him for it, he has fulfilled its thanks."

Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned that Bukhtanassar brought Daniel, and he ordered him to be imprisoned in a well and set two lions upon him, then left them between him and himself. Then after five days he opened it and found him standing and praying while the two lions were in a corner of the well and had not approached him. He said to him: "What did you say when you were pushed upon?" He said: "I said: 'Praise be to Allah, who does not forget whoever remembers Him. Praise be to Allah, who does not disappoint whoever hopes in Him. Praise be to Allah, who does not leave whoever relies upon Him to other than Him. Praise be to Allah, who is our trust when all means are cut off from us. Praise be to Allah, who is our hope when our opinion of our deeds is bad. Praise be to Allah, who removes our harm after our distress. Praise be to Allah, who rewards kindness with kindness. Praise be to Allah, who rewards patience with deliverance.'"

It is related from him (Daniel) that when he looked into the mirror he said: "Praise be to Allah, who has made my creation and my character good, and has made beautiful in me what made others ugly."

Ibn Sirin said: "Ibn Umar used to look much into the mirror, and he would be with it on journeys. I said to him: 'Why?' He said: 'I look, and whatever beauty is in my face, it is a blemish in the face of others. I praise Allah for it.'"

Abu Bakr ibn Abi Maryam was asked what the completion of blessing is. He said: "That you place one foot on the Sirat and one foot in Paradise."

Bakr ibn Abd Allah said: "O son of Adam, if you wish to know the measure of what Allah has bestowed upon you, close your eyes."

Muqatil, regarding His saying ﴿And He has lavished upon you His favours, outward and inward﴾ said: "As for the outward, it is Islam; as for the inward, it is His concealing your sins."

Ibn Shawdhab said: Abd Allah, meaning Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Allah has a favour upon the people of the Fire. If He wished to punish them with something harsher than the Fire, He would have punished them."

Abu Sulayman al-Darani said: "The companions of the Most Merciful on the Day of Resurrection are those in whom are these qualities: generosity, liberality, forbearance, tenderness, mercy, gratitude, righteousness, and patience."

Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Whoever sees a person afflicted and says: 'Praise be to Allah who has spared me from what He has afflicted you with, and has preferred me over you and over much of His creation,' has fulfilled the thanks for that blessing."

Abd Allah ibn Wahb said: "I heard Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd say: 'Gratitude takes hold of the root and the origin of praise, and its branch.' He said: 'One looks at Allah's blessings in his body, his hearing, his sight, his hands, his feet, and other things. There is nothing of this but that it contains a blessing from Allah. It is incumbent upon the servant to act, by obedience to Allah, with the blessing that is in his body; and another blessing is in provision, and it is incumbent upon him to act for Allah with what He has bestowed upon him of provision, by obeying Him. Whoever acts according to this has taken hold of the root of gratitude, its origin and its branch.'"

Ka'b said: "No servant has been given a blessing in this world and has thanked Allah for it and been humble before Allah for it, except that Allah gives him its benefit in this world and raises for him a degree in the Hereafter. And no servant has been given a blessing in this world and has not thanked Allah for it and has not been humble for it, except that Allah withholds its benefit in this world, opens for him layers of the Fire, and punishes him if He wills, or pardons him."

Al-Hasan said: "Whoever does not see that Allah has a blessing upon him except in food, drink, or clothing, his knowledge is deficient and his punishment is present."

Al-Hasan said one day to Bakr al-Muzani: "Speak, Abu Abd Allah, supplications for your brothers." He praised Allah, extolled Him, invoked blessings upon the Prophet, and then said: "By Allah, I do not know which of the two blessings is better for me and for you: the blessing of the path (al-maslak) or the blessing of the exit (al-makhraj) when He brings it out from us." Al-Hasan said: "Indeed, it is from the blessing of food."

Ayisha (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "No servant drinks plain water, enters it without harm and expels it without harm, except that gratitude becomes obligatory upon him."

Al-Hasan (al-Basri) said: "How great a blessing it is, that it enters and brings every pleasure, and expels what is harmful. There was once a king of the kings of this town who would see one of his slave boys come with a water-jug, measure from it, and then drink standing. He would say: 'Would that I were like you, drinking until your thirst is cut off!' When he drank, that single drink was for him a hundred deaths. How great a blessing!"

Some scholars wrote to a brother of theirs: "Indeed, we have awoken to the favours of Allah, which we cannot count, along with our many acts of disobedience. So we do not know which we should be grateful for: the beauty that He has made easy for us, or the ugliness that He has concealed."

It was said to al-Hasan: "There is a man here who does not sit with people." So he came to him and asked him about this. He said: "I spend my evenings and mornings between a sin and a favour. So I decided to occupy myself, away from people, with seeking forgiveness for the sin and thanking Allah for the favour." Al-Hasan said to him: "O servant of Allah, in my view you are more learned in jurisprudence than al-Hasan. So hold fast to what you are upon."

Ibn al-Mubarak said: "I heard Ali ibn Salih say, concerning the words of the Exalted ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾: 'That is, [an increase] from My obedience.'"

The verification is that the increase is of blessings, and that His obedience is for the sake of His blessings.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya mentioned that Muharib ibn Dithar used to stand in prayer at night and sometimes raise his voice: "I am the little one whom You raised, so to You be praise. I am the weak one whom You strengthened, so to You be praise. I am the poor one whom You made rich, so to You be praise. I am the destitute one whom You provided for, so to You be praise. I am the unmarried one whom You married off, so to You be praise. I am the hungry one whom You fed, so to You be praise. I am the naked one whom You clothed, so to You be praise. I am the traveller whom You accompanied, so to You be praise. I am the absent one whom You returned, so to You be praise. I am the one on foot whom You carried, so to You be praise. I am the sick one whom You cured, so to You be praise. I am the one who asked and whom You gave, so to You be praise. I am the one who called upon You and whom You answered, so to You be praise. Our Lord, and to You be praise, abundant praise."

Some preachers used to say in their sermon: "He shaped the nose for you, raised it up, perfected it, and made its perfection beautiful. Then He fashioned the pupil of your eye, placed it between closed eyelids and hanging lashes. He moved you from stage to stage, and He caused the hearts of your parents to be tender and affectionate toward you. So His favours upon you are blossoming, and His bounties surround you."

Some scholars used to say concerning the words of the Exalted ﴿And if you tried to count the favours of Allah, you could not enumerate them﴾: "Glory be to Him, who has not made the knowledge of His favours attainable for anyone except the knowledge of one's shortcoming in knowing them. Just as He has not made the perception of anyone exceed the knowledge that he cannot perceive Him. So He made the recognition of His favours, along with the acknowledgement of one's shortcoming in recognising them, a form of gratitude. Just as the knowledge of the knowers that they cannot comprehend Him is itself thanks to Him, and He made it a form of faith, knowing that the servants cannot go beyond this."

Ibn al-Mubarak said: Mathna ibn al-Sabah related to us from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Two qualities, whoever possesses them, Allah records him as patient and grateful; and whoever does not possess them, Allah does not record him as patient and grateful: one who looks at his religion to those above him and follows their example, and one who looks at his worldly affairs to those below him.'"

[And] whoever praises Allah for what He has favoured him with, Allah records him as patient and grateful. And whoever looks at his religion to those below him, and looks at his worldly affairs to those above him, and grieves over what has escaped him of it, Allah does not record him as patient and grateful.

Through the same chain, from Abdullah ibn Amr, as a mawquf (a report ending with a Companion, not traced to the Prophet): "Four qualities: whoever has them, Allah builds for him a house in Paradise. Whoever has as the safeguard of his affair 'There is no god but Allah'; when a calamity strikes him he says, 'Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we return'; when he is given something he says, 'Praise be to Allah'; and when he sins he says, 'I seek the forgiveness of Allah.'"

Ibn al-Mubarak related from Shibl, from Abu Najih, from Mujahid, concerning the words of the Exalted ﴿Indeed he was a grateful servant﴾: "He would not eat anything without praising Allah for it, nor drink any drink without praising Allah for it, nor lay hold of anything without praising Allah for it. So Allah praised him: Indeed he was a grateful servant."

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "Nuh (peace be upon him), when he ate, said, 'Praise be to Allah'; when he drank, said, 'Praise be to Allah'; when he dressed, said, 'Praise be to Allah'; and when he rode, said, 'Praise be to Allah.' So Allah named him a grateful servant."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya said: It reached me from some wise men who said: "If Allah had not punished for disobedience to Him, it would still have been fitting that He not be disobeyed, out of gratitude for His favour."

(Section)

For Allah, Blessed and Exalted, upon His servant there are two kinds of rights that never separate from him:

The first: His commands and prohibitions, which are purely His right over him.

The second: the thanks for His favours which He has bestowed upon him. So He, glory be to Him, requires of him thanks for His favours and the performance of His command. The witnessing of what is obligatory upon him keeps showing him his shortcoming and his neglect, and that he is in need of Allah's pardon and forgiveness. If he is not overtaken by this, he is ruined. The more a person understands the religion of Allah, the more complete his witnessing of what is obligatory upon him, and the greater his witnessing of his own shortcoming. Religion is not merely the abandonment of the apparent prohibited acts, but also, together with that, the performance of the commands that are beloved to Allah. Most of the religious do not concern themselves except with what they share with the general mass of people.

As for jihad, enjoining good, forbidding evil, sincere counsel to Allah, His Messenger and His servants, and supporting Allah, His Messenger, His religion and His Book, these obligations do not even occur to them, let alone that they intend to perform them or actually perform them. The least religious of people, and the most despised by Allah, are those who abandon these obligations, even if they renounce the entire world. Rarely will you find among them one whose face reddens and darkens for Allah, who becomes angry for the sake of His sacred limits, or who sacrifices his honour in supporting his religion. The people of major sins are in a better state with Allah than these. Abu Umar (Ibn Abd al-Barr) and others mentioned that Allah commanded one of the angels to sink a town into the earth. He said: "O Lord, among them is so-and-so, the worshipper and ascetic." He said: "Begin with him, and let me hear his voice, for his face has never once darkened [for Me]."

(Section)

As for witnessing the favour, it leaves him no good deed of his own in view at all, even if he performed the deeds of both humans and jinn. For the favours of Allah, glory be to Him, are more numerous than his deeds, and the least of His favours outweighs his deeds. So the servant should not cease to look at the right that Allah has over him.

Imam Ahmad said: Hajjaj related to us, Jarir ibn Hazim related to us, from Wahb, who said: "It reached me that the Prophet of Allah Musa (peace be upon him) passed by a man who was supplicating and humbling himself. He said: 'O Lord, have mercy upon him, for I have had mercy on him.' So Allah revealed to him: 'Even if he calls upon Me until his strength is cut off, I will not respond to him until he looks into My right over him.'"

So the servant's witnessing of the favour and of the obligation leaves him no good deed that he sees in himself. He keeps belittling himself and blaming his soul. How near such a person is to mercy, if he gives each of these two witnessings its due. And Allah is the One sought for help.

(Section: on judging between the two groups and distinguishing between the two parties)

We say: whenever two matters are sought to be weighed against each other, and the heavier of them over the lighter is to be known, this cannot be done except after knowing each of them. We have already mentioned the reality of patience and its divisions and types, and now we will mention the reality of gratitude and its essence.

In al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari) it says: "Shukr (gratitude) is praise of the benefactor for the kindness he has bestowed. One says: shakartuhu and shakartu lahu (with the lam), the latter being more eloquent." The words of the Exalted ﴿We do not want from you reward or thanks﴾ may be a verbal noun like qu'ud (sitting), or may be a plural like burud (blankets) and kufur (ingratitude). Shukran is the opposite of kufran (ingratitude). Tashakkartu lahu is like shakartu lahu. Shakur among animals is one that is satisfied with little fodder. Ishtakarat al-sama' means the rain of the sky became intense. Ishtakara al-dar' means the udder became full of milk. One says from it: shakarat al-naqatu (the she-camel) becomes grateful, she is shakira, and shakarat al-shajaratu (the tree) grows shakir when the shakir (new shoots) emerges from it, which is what grows around the tree from its root.

Reflect on this derivation and match it with the gratitude that is commanded, and with the gratitude which is the reward of the Lord, the Grateful. You will find in all of them the meaning of increase and growth. It is also said of an animal that it is shakur when it shows more fat than it is given as fodder.

The gratitude of the servant revolves around three pillars, and he is not grateful unless all three are together: first, his acknowledgment of Allah's favour upon him; second, praising Him for it; and third, using it to seek His pleasure.

As for what people have said about gratitude: one group said it is the acknowledgment of the Bestower's favours in a state of humility. It was also said: gratitude is praising the benefactor by mentioning his kindness to you, so the servant's gratitude is his praise of Him by mentioning His kindness to him. It was also said: gratitude for a favour is witnessing the grace, guarding the sanctity, and performing the service. It was also said: gratitude for a favour is that you see yourself as a parasite upon it. It was also said: gratitude is recognising one's inability to be grateful. It is said: thanking Allah for being grateful is more complete than gratitude itself; that is, you see your gratitude as His enabling, and that enabling is among the greatest of favours upon you, so you thank Him for the gratitude, and then you thank Him for the thanks, unless you see yourself as worthy of the favour. It was also said: gratitude is exhausting one's capacity in obedience. It was also said: the grateful (shakir) is one who gives thanks for what exists, and the very grateful (shakur) is one who gives thanks for what is lost. It was also said: the grateful is one who gives thanks for provision received, and the very grateful is one who gives thanks for provision withheld. It was also said: the grateful is one who gives thanks for benefit, and the very grateful is one who gives thanks for deprivation. It was also said: the grateful is one who gives thanks for a gift, and the very grateful is one who gives thanks for a trial.

Al-Junayd said: "I was playing before al-Sari (al-Saqati) when I was seven years old. Among us was a group speaking about gratitude. He said to me: 'O boy, what is gratitude?' I said: 'That you do not disobey Allah with His favours.' He said: 'Soon your share from Allah will be your tongue.' I have not stopped weeping over this word that al-Sari said."

Al-Shibli said: "Gratitude is seeing the Bestower, not seeing the favours." This is not good. Rather, it is part of the completeness of gratitude that you witness the favour as coming from the Bestower.

It was also said: gratitude is the binding of what exists and the hunting of what is lost.

Abu Uthman said: "The gratitude of the common people is for food and clothing, and the gratitude of the elite is for the meanings that come to their hearts."

A sultan imprisoned a man, and his companion sent to him: "Give thanks to Allah!" Then he was beaten, and he sent to him again: "Give thanks to Allah!" Then there was brought in a Magian prisoner suffering from dysentery. He was shackled, and a ring of his shackle was placed on his leg and a ring on the aforementioned man's leg. The Magian would stand up at night several times, so the man had to stand over his head until he had finished. His companion wrote to him: "Give thanks to Allah!" He said to him: "Until when will you say 'Give thanks to Allah'? What trial is greater than this?" [The reply came]: "If the zunnar (the belt worn by Magians) that is at his waist were placed at your waist just as the shackle on his leg has been placed on your leg, what would you do? So give thanks to Allah."

A man entered upon Sahl ibn Abdullah and said: "A thief entered my house and took my goods." He said: "Give thanks to Allah! If the thief had entered your heart, which is Satan, and corrupted your tawhid (monotheism) for you, what would you have done?"

It was also said: gratitude is the enjoyment of praising Him for what one does not deserve from His giving. It was also said: if your hand falls short of repaying, let your tongue lengthen in gratitude. It was also said: four things have no fruit: consulting the deaf, placing a favour with one who does not thank for it, sowing seed in salt marsh, and a lamp in the sunlight.

Gratitude is connected to the heart, the tongue and the limbs. The heart is for recognition and love, the tongue is for praise and commendation, and the limbs are for using them in obedience to the One who is thanked and restraining them from His disobedience. A poet said:

"Three of my favours have benefited you: my hand, my tongue, and the hidden heart."

Gratitude is more specific to actions, and praise is more specific to words. The cause of praise is more general than the cause of gratitude. What is the object of gratitude and that by which gratitude is expressed is more general than that by which praise is expressed. So what the Lord, exalted is He, is praised for is more general than what He is thanked for, for He is praised for His names, attributes, actions and favours, and He is thanked for His favours. And what praise is expressed by is more specific than what gratitude is expressed by, for gratitude is expressed by the heart, the tongue and the limbs, while praise is expressed by the heart and the tongue.

(Section) Having understood this: each of patience and gratitude is included within the reality of the other, and neither can exist without the other. Each is named by its specific name according to what predominates in it and is most apparent in it. Otherwise, the reality of gratitude is composed of patience, intention and action. For gratitude is acting in obedience to Allah and abstaining from His disobedience, and patience is the foundation of that. So patience in obedience and patience against disobedience is itself gratitude. And when patience is commanded, its fulfilment is gratitude.

If it is said: this implies the unity of patience and gratitude, and that they are two names for one referent, which is impossible rationally, linguistically and conventionally, and Allah has distinguished between them?

It is answered: rather, they are two distinct meanings. We have only shown their mutual entailment and that each one's essential reality depends on the other. Whenever gratitude is stripped of patience, it ceases to be gratitude; and whenever patience is stripped of gratitude, it ceases to be patience. As for the first, it is evident. As for the second, if patience is stripped of gratitude, it becomes ingratitude (kufur), and the opposition of ingratitude to patience is greater than the opposition of discontent (sakhat).

If it is said: rather, there is another category, namely that a person is neither ungrateful nor grateful, but patient with reluctance and strong aversion. Such a person has not attained the reality of gratitude, but has not left the reality of patience. It is answered: our discussion concerns the patience that is commanded and is obedience, not the patience which is mere endurance, like the patience of animals. The patience of obedience is not performed except by a grateful person, but his gratitude is absorbed into his patience, so the ruling belongs to patience, just as the patience of a very grateful person is absorbed into his gratitude, so the ruling belongs to gratitude. The stations of faith are not annihilated by moving through them; rather, they are absorbed, and the lower is contained within the higher, just as faith is absorbed into excellence (ihsan). And just as patience is absorbed into the stations of contentment (rida), not that patience disappears and contentment is absorbed into surrender (tafwid), and fear and hope are absorbed into love, not that they disappear.

A single decreed matter may be connected to both gratitude and patience, whether it is beloved or disliked. Poverty, for example, is connected to patience, which is most specific to it because of the aversion in it, and it is connected to gratitude because of the favour in it. Whoever witnesses his favour predominantly, and takes pleasure in it, rests, and is content with it, counts it as a favour for which he gives thanks. Whoever witnesses predominantly the trial, the constraint and the need in it, counts it as an affliction for which he is patient. The reverse is true of wealth.

Moreover, Allah, glory be to Him, tested the servants with blessings just as He tested them with calamities, and He called all of that a trial. He said: ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾. And He said: ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him and honours him and blesses him, he says: My Lord has honoured me. But when He tests him and restricts his provision, he says: My Lord has humiliated me.﴾

And He said: ﴿Indeed, We have made what is upon the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed.﴾ And He said: ﴿He who created death and life that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed.﴾ And He said: ﴿And He it is who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the water, that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed.﴾ So He informed that He created the upper world and the lower world, and decreed the term of creation, and created what is upon the earth for trial and testing. This trial is nothing but the trial of the servants' patience and gratitude in good and evil, in ease and hardship. So the trial by blessings, such as wealth, health, rank and power, and the trial by afflictions, both come. The greater of the two trials is the trial of ease, and the more difficult of the two patiences is patience in obedience to Allah. As the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) said: "We were tested with adversity and we were patient; we were tested with ease and we were not patient." And blessings may take the form of poverty, sickness, the withdrawal of this world and its means, and harm from people; these may be the greater of the two blessings, and gratitude for them is more obligatory than gratitude for their opposites. So the Lord, exalted is He, tests with His blessings and blesses with His tests. However, patience and gratitude are two states that are necessarily attached to the servant in the matter of the Lord's command, prohibition, decree and destiny, and he cannot do without them for the blink of an eye. To ask which of them is better is like asking which is better: sensation or movement; or food or drink; or the servant's fear or his hope. The commanded act is not performed except with patience and gratitude, and the forbidden act is not abandoned except with patience and gratitude. As for the decreed calamities that befall the servant, whenever he is patient with them, his gratitude is absorbed into his patience, just as the patience of the grateful is absorbed into his gratitude.

What clarifies this is that Allah, glory be to Him, tested the servant through his own self and his desire, and obligated him to struggle against them for Allah's sake. So he is at every moment struggling against his self until it performs the gratitude that is commanded, and remains patient against the desire whose obedience is forbidden. The servant is never free of these two, whether he is rich or poor, healthy or afflicted. This is the question of the rich grateful person versus the poor patient person: which is better? People have three opinions on this. [The scholars] who mentioned Abu al-Faraj Ibn al-Jawzi and others on the general question of which is better, patience or gratitude, each group argued for its view with proofs and evidence.

The verification is to say: the better of the two is the one more God-fearing, for if they are equal in piety, they are equal in merit. For Allah, glory be to Him, did not prefer by poverty or wealth, just as He did not prefer by health or affliction. Rather, He preferred by piety, as He said: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you.﴾ He also said: "No Arab has any merit over a non-Arab, and no non-Arab has any merit over an Arab, except by piety. People are from Adam, and Adam was from dust." Piety is built upon two foundations: patience and gratitude. Each of the rich and the poor must have both. So whoever has the more complete patience and gratitude is the better.

If it is said: then if the poor person's patience is more complete and the rich person's gratitude is more complete, which of them is better?

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 1, verse 2 (part 12 of 14):

It has been said: [The more excellent of the two is] the one who is more dutiful to Allah in his obligation and in what his state requires. Preference cannot be made in any other way at all. For the rich man may be more dutiful to Allah in his thankfulness than the poor man in his patience, and the poor man may be more dutiful to Allah in his patience than the rich man in his thankfulness. So it is not correct to say that this one is better for his wealth, nor that this one is better for his poverty, nor is it correct to say that this one is better in thankfulness than that one in patience, or the reverse, because they are both vehicles (mataya) for faith, and both are necessary. Rather, the correct statement is: the one who is more upright in the obligatory duties and the recommended acts is the more excellent, for preference follows these two matters, as Allah the Exalted said in the divine hadith: "My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him, and My servant continues to draw near to Me through voluntary acts until I love him." So whichever of the two men was more upright in the obligations and more abundant in voluntary acts, he is the more excellent.

If it is said: It has been established from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The poor among my community will enter Paradise before their rich by half a day, and that is five hundred years." It is said: This does not indicate their superiority over the rich in rank and elevation of station. Even if they precede them in entering, the rich or the just ruler may be delayed in entering because of his reckoning. When he enters, his rank is higher and his station more elevated, like the poor man who precedes the (laden) camel in narrow passages and other places, while the one with burdens comes after him.

If it is said: The Prophet said to the poor, when they complained to him of the rich outdoing them in acts such as freeing slaves and giving charity: "Shall I not direct you to something which, if you do it, you will overtake those who preceded you?" So he directed them to glorifying (tasbih), praising (tahmid) and magnifying (takbir) Allah after every prayer. When the rich heard of this, they practised it, and they reported that to the Prophet, and he said: "That is the bounty of Allah, which He gives to whom He wills." This indicates the preference of the state of the thankful rich. It is said: This is an argument for the view we have supported, namely that the more excellent of the two is the one with more voluntary acts. If they are equal, they are equal. Here, the rich have equalled the poor in their obligatory and voluntary acts, and exceeded them with the voluntary acts of freeing slaves and giving charity, and so they surpassed them in that. They equalled them in their patience in jihad, in enduring harm for the sake of Allah, and in patience with what is decreed, and they exceeded them in thankfulness through voluntary acts of wealth. Had the poor had voluntary acts in their patience exceeding the voluntary acts of the rich, they would have surpassed them thereby.

If it is said: The Prophet was offered the keys of the treasures of this world, and he refused them and said: "Rather, I will be satisfied one day and hungry one day." And Hisham ibn 'Urwah narrated from his father, from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "The Messenger of Allah departed from this world without having been satisfied with wheat bread, and he died while his armour was pawned to a Jew for food he had taken for his family."

Imam Ahmad said: Waki' narrated to us, al-A'mash narrated to us, from 'Ubadah ibn al-Qa'qa', from Abu Zur'ah, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah said: "O Allah, make the provision of the family of Muhammad sustenance (qut)."

Imam Ahmad said: Isma'il ibn Muhammad narrated to us, 'Abbad ibn 'Abbad narrated to us, Mujalid ibn Sa'id narrated to us, from al-Sha'bi, from Masruq, from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: A woman of the Ansar entered upon me and saw the bed of the Prophet, a folded cloak, so she returned to her house and sent me a mattress stuffed with wool. The Prophet entered upon me and said: "What is this?" I said: "So-and-so, the Ansari woman, entered upon me, saw your bed, and sent me this." He said: "Return it." I did not return it, and I liked that it should be in my house. He said that to me three times, then he said: "O 'A'ishah, return it, for by Allah, if I wished, Allah would have made mountains of gold and silver walk with me." So I returned it. And Allah, glorified is He, would not choose for His Messenger except the more excellent. Moreover, if he had taken the world, he would have spent it all in seeking the pleasure of Allah, and his thankfulness with it would have been above the thankfulness of all the worlds.

It is said: Each of the two groups has argued from the state of the Messenger of Allah. The truth is that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, combined for him both stations in their completeness: he was the master of the thankful rich and the master of the patient poor. He attained from patience in poverty what no one else attained, and from thankfulness in wealth what no wealthy person other than him attained. Whoever reflects on his biography will find it to be so. He was the most patient of creation in the situations calling for patience and the most thankful of creation in the situations calling for thankfulness. His Lord, exalted is He, perfected for him the degrees of perfection, placing him in the highest rank of the thankful rich and in the highest rank of the patient poor. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And He found you poor and made you rich﴾. The commentators agreed that the 'a'il (ʿāʾil) is the poor man; it is said: 'āla al-rajul ya'īlu when he became poor; and a'āla ya'īlu when he became one with dependents, like labana and athmara (he became one with milk and one with fruit), and athra when he became one with abundance and wealth. And 'āla ya'ūlu when he oppressed, and from it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿That is closer to your not being unjust (ta'ūlū)﴾.

It has been said that the meaning is "that you not have many dependents," but the first view is correct, for several reasons.

The first: It is not known in the language that 'āla ya'ūlu means "he had many dependents." What is known in that sense is 'āla ya'īlu. As for 'āla ya'ūlu, it means only "to oppress," and this is what all the lexicographers have mentioned without exception.

The second: He, glorified is He, paired that with justice, which removes them, when they fear failing to be just, to a single wife, or to concubinage with whatever they wish of what their right hands possess. Here, explaining it by the absence of dependents is not fitting.

The third reinforces this: He, glorified is He, moved them, when they feared not being equitable regarding marrying orphans, to other women besides them, lest they wrong their orphan wives. He permitted them to marry one, or two, up to four. Then He moved them, when they feared oppression and failure to be equitable in division, to one wife, or to the kind over whom there is no division in enjoyment, namely their slave-women. Thus the verse comprises the explanation of what is permitted of marrying orphans and of mature women, and of the more preferable of those two options when justice is feared. So the multiplicity of dependents has no place here at all.

The fourth reinforces this: If the thing feared were a multiplicity of dependents, He would not have moved them to whatever they wished of an unlimited number of slave-women, for dependents are as much from wives as from slave-women, and there is no difference. Rather, He did not move them to slave-women for service, but to slave-women for concubinage.

The fifth reinforces this: A multiplicity of dependents is not a matter that is disliked or abhorrent to the Lord, the Exalted. How could it be, when the best of this community is the one with the most women? The Prophet said: "Marry the loving and the fertile, for I will boast of you before the nations." So he commanded marrying the fertile, so that there might come from them what he would boast of before the nations on the Day of Resurrection.

The purpose is that He, glorified is He, made His Prophet rich and thankful after he had been poor and patient. So no group may argue from his state for its own condition without the other group being entitled to argue from it likewise for its own condition.

If it is said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf (may Allah be pleased with him) was among the thankful, and Imam Ahmad said in his Musnad: 'Abd al-Samad narrated to us, 'Ammarah narrated to us, from Thabit, from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: While 'A'ishah was in her house, she heard a sound in Madinah and said: "What is this?" They said: "A caravan of 'Abd al-Rahman's, it has arrived from Syria carrying everything." He said: There were seven hundred camels, and Madinah was shaken by the noise. 'A'ishah said: I heard the Messenger of Allah say: "I saw 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf entering Paradise crawling." This reached 'Abd al-Rahman, and he said: "If I can, I will enter it standing." So he gave all of it, with its loads and saddles, in the way of Allah.

It is said: Imam Ahmad said this hadith is a lie and munkar. They said: Or 'Ammarah narrates munkar hadiths. Abu Hatim al-Razi said: 'Ammarah ibn Zadhan is not to be used as proof.

Abu al-Faraj said: al-Jarrah ibn al-Minhal narrated with his chain from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf that the Prophet said to him: "O Ibn 'Awf, you are among the rich, and you will not enter Paradise except crawling, so lend to your Lord and He will free your feet." Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Nasa'i said: This hadith is fabricated (mawdu'), and al-Jarrah is abandoned in hadith (matruk al-hadith). Yahya said: The hadith of al-Jarrah is worth nothing. Ibn al-Madini said: His hadith is not to be written down. Ibn Hibban said: He used to lie. al-Daraqutni said: Abandoned (matruk).

If it is said: What will you do with the hadith narrated by al-Bayhaqi from the hadith of Ahmad ibn 'Ali ibn Isma'il ibn Muhammad: Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, Khalid ibn Yazid ibn Abi Malik informed me, from his father, from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, from Ibrahim ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, from his father, that the Prophet said: "O Ibn 'Awf, you are among the rich, and you will not enter Paradise except crawling, so lend to Allah and He will free your feet." He said: "What should I lend, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "You disown what you have become in." He said: "All of it, all together, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Yes." So he went out grieving over that, and Gabriel came to him and said: "Command Ibn 'Awf to host the guest, feed the poor, begin with those he supports, and give to the beggar. When he does that, it will be a purification of what he is in."

It is said: This hadith is false and is not authentically from the Messenger of Allah, for one of its narrators, Khalid ibn Yazid ibn Abi Malik, Imam Ahmad said: "He is nothing." Ibn Ma'in said: "Weak (wahin)." al-Nasa'i said: "Not trustworthy." al-Daraqutni said: "Weak." Yahya ibn Ma'in said: "He did not accept lying about his father until he lied about the Companions."

If it is said: What will you do with the hadith that Imam Ahmad said: al-Hudhayl ibn Maymun narrated to us, from Mutarrif ibn Yazid, from 'Ubaydullah ibn Zahr, from 'Ali ibn Yazid, from al-Qasim, from Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah said: "I entered Paradise and heard a rustling before me. I said: 'What is this?' He said: 'Bilal.' I went on, and there were most of the people of Paradise the poor emigrants and the offspring of the Muslims. I did not see among them anyone fewer than the rich and the women. It was said to me: 'As for the rich, they are at the gate being reckoned and purified; and as for the women, the two reds, gold and silk, have distracted them.' Then we went out through one of the eight gates of Paradise. When I was near the gate, a scale was brought and I was placed in one pan, and my community in the other pan, and I outweighed them. Then Abu Bakr was brought and placed in one pan, and all my community was brought and placed in the other pan, and Abu Bakr outweighed them. Then 'Umar was brought and placed in one pan, and my community in the other pan, and 'Umar outweighed them. My community was presented to me man by man, and they kept passing, but I was slow to see 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf. Then he came after despair, and I said: 'Abd al-Rahman. He said: 'My father and mother be ransom for you, O Messenger of Allah. By the One who sent you with truth, I did not reach you until I thought I would not reach you except after the difficult ones.' I said: 'And what is that?' He said: 'From the abundance of my wealth, I was being reckoned and purified.'"

It is said: This hadith cannot be used as proof by its chain. Abu al-Faraj included both it and the previous one in his book of fabricated hadiths. He said: As for 'Ubaydullah ibn Zahr, Yahya said: "He is nothing." And 'Ali ibn Yazid is abandoned. Ibn Hibban said: "'Ubaydullah narrates fabrications from the reliable narrators, and when he narrates from 'Ali ibn Yazid he brings abominations, and when the reports of 'Ubaydullah ibn Zahr, 'Ali ibn Yazid and al-Qasim ibn 'Abd al-Rahman are combined in one chain, the text of that report is nothing but what their hands have made."

Abu al-Faraj said: With this false hadith, the whole class of ascetics attach themselves, and they consider wealth an obstacle to precedence in good. They say: "If Ibn 'Awf enters Paradise crawling because of his wealth, that is sufficient to condemn wealth." But the hadith is not authentic. Far be it that 'Abd al-Rahman, who was testified to for Paradise, should have his wealth prevent him from precedence, for gathering wealth is permissible; what is blameworthy is earning it from an unlawful source and withholding the due right in it. 'Abd al-Rahman is free of both states. Talhah left three hundred loads of gold, and al-Zubayr and others left wealth too. Had they known that this was blameworthy, they would have given away everything. How many a storyteller presents such a hadith, urging poverty and condemning wealth! May Allah reward the scholars who know the authentic and understand the principles. End.

I say: He went to great lengths in refuting this hadith and exceeded the limit in classing it among the fabricated, invented hadiths against the Messenger of Allah. It seems he regarded as very grave the delay of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, who is one of the foremost early Muslims testified to for precedence in entering Paradise and for entering it crawling, and he considered that a contradiction of his precedence and the rank that Allah prepared for him in Paradise. This is an error on his part, may Allah have mercy on him.

Suppose he found a way to impugn these two reports; would he find a way to discredit the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah said: "The poor among the Muslims will enter Paradise before their rich by half a day, and that is five hundred years." al-Tirmidhi said: "A hasan sahih hadith."

In the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, which Muslim narrated in his Sahih, from the Prophet: "The poor emigrants will precede the rich on the Day of Resurrection by forty autumns."

In the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, from him, from the Prophet: "Do you know who will enter Paradise first?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "The poor emigrants, those through whom hardships are averted, one of whom dies while his need is in his chest, unable to fulfil it."

In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Jabir (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet, that he said: "The poor among my community will enter Paradise before the rich by forty autumns." This hadith and its like are sound and explicit about the precedence of the poor Companions over their rich, though they vary in their precedence: some precede by five hundred years, and others by forty years. That does not detract from the rank of those who entered later, for they may have a higher rank than those who preceded them into entry, even if they came after them for reckoning. The just ruler is held for reckoning, and someone who has held no affairs of the Muslims precedes him into Paradise. When the just ruler enters after him, his rank is higher than the rank of the poor man. Indeed, he will be among the people nearest to Allah in rank, as in Sahih Muslim, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet, who said: "Those who act justly with Allah on the Day of Resurrection will be on pulpits of light at the right hand of the Merciful, and both His hands are right, those who are just in their judgment, their families, and what they govern." In the Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet: "The people most beloved to Allah on the Day of Resurrection and nearest to Him in sitting is a just imam, and the people most hated by Allah on the Day of Resurrection and most severe in punishment is an oppressive imam." So the just imam and the rich man may each be delayed in entering for reckoning, and after entering, be higher in rank than the earlier poor man. The delay of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf because of the abundance of his wealth, until he is reckoned for it and then joins the Messenger of Allah and his Companions, does not bring him any disgrace or diminish his rank, nor does it contradict his precedence or his being testified to for Paradise. As for the hadith of his entering Paradise crawling, the matter is as Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said of it: it is a lie and munkar; and as al-Nasa'i said: it is fabricated. The stations of 'Abd al-Rahman, his jihad, his great expenditures and his charities require that he enter with those who pass like lightning, or like a glance, or like the finest horses, and that He not leave him to enter crawling.

(Section)

Allah, glorified is He, just as He is the Creator of creation, is also the Creator of that by which they have their wealth and their poverty.

He created wealth and poverty to test His servants with them, which of them is best in deed, and made them a cause for obedience and disobedience, reward and punishment. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial, and to Us you will be returned﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "With hardship and ease, health and sickness, wealth and poverty, the lawful and the unlawful, and all of it is a trial." Ibn Yazid said: "We test you with what you love and what you dislike, to see how your patience and your thankfulness are, with what you love and what you dislike." al-Kalbi said: "With evil: with poverty and affliction; and with good: with wealth and children." So He, glorified is He, informed that wealth and poverty are the two vehicles of trial and examination. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him and honours him and blesses him, he says: "My Lord has honoured me." But when He tests him and restricts his provision, he says: "My Lord has humiliated me." No indeed!﴾

So He informed that He tests His servant by honouring him, by blessing him and by extending provision to him, just as He tests him by restricting provision and measuring it out to him, and that both are a trial and examination from Him. Then He denounced those who claimed that the extension and widening of provision is an honour from Allah to His servant, and that its restriction is a humiliation from Him to him. He said "No indeed," meaning: the matter is not as man says; rather he has been tested by My blessing, and blessed by My trial.

If you reflect on the wording of the verse, you will find this meaning shining clearly on its pages for the one who reflects. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And it is He who has made you successors upon the earth and raised some of you above others in degrees, to test you in what He has given you﴾. And the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed﴾. So He informed that He adorned the earth with what is on it of wealth and other things for trial and examination, just as He informed that He created death and life for that purpose, and created the heavens and the earth also for this trial. These are three places in the Qur'an in which He, glorified is He, informs that He created the upper and lower world and what is between them, and the term of the world and the term of its people, and the causes of their livelihoods, which He made an adornment of the earth: gold and silver, dwellings, clothing, mounts, crops, fruits, animals, women, sons, and other things. All of that He created for trial and examination, that He might test His creation as to which of them is most obedient to Him and most pleasing to Him. He is the Best in deed.

This is the truth by which the heavens and the earth and what is between them were created, and for which they exist. Its purpose is reward and punishment. To neglect it and render it void would be the vanity from which He has declared Himself exalted, and He has informed us that He is高 above it. His dominion is true, He alone is God, and He alone is Lord of everything. This negates the false assumption and the baseless reckoning, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Did you think that We created you without purpose, and that you would not be returned to Us? So exalted is Allah, the True King. There is no god but Him, the Lord of the Mighty Throne.﴾

He, glorified be He, has exalted Himself above that, just as He has exalted Himself above partners, offspring, consorts, and all other defects and deficiencies: drowsiness, sleep, weariness, and need. He is also exalted above being burdened by preserving the heavens and the earth, and above intercessors coming before Him without His permission, as His polytheist enemies suppose. Nor does He lose knowledge of the particulars of the world, or of any part of them. Just as His perfect majesty and the perfection of His names and attributes reject this, they also prevent Him from creating His servants in vain and leaving them neglected, without commanding or forbidding them, and without returning them to Himself, so that He would reward the good among them for their goodness and the evildoer for his evil. Then the wrongdoers would know that they had been liars, and He would show them that His messengers and their followers were more deserving of truth and righteousness than they were. Whoever denies this has denied His divinity, His lordship, and His true dominion, and that is the very essence of disbelief and rejection of Him, glorified be He. As the believer said to his companion who debated with him about the Return and denied it: ﴿Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then fashioned you into a man?﴾ He informed us that denying the Return is disbelief in the very essence of the Lord, glorified be He. Allah the Exalted also said: ﴿And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying: "When we are dust, shall we indeed be in a new creation?" Those are the ones who disbelieved in their Lord.﴾ This is because denying the Return implies denying the power, knowledge, and wisdom of the Lord, His true dominion, His lordship, and His divinity. Likewise, denying His messengers and rejecting their message implies the same. Whoever denies His messengers and rejects the Return has denied His lordship, glorified be He, and has negated that He is the Lord of the worlds.

The point is that He, glorified and exalted be He, created wealth and poverty as two mounts for trial and testing, and He did not send down wealth merely for enjoyment. As in the Musnad (of Imam Ahmad), from him (Ibn Mas'ud?) who said: Allah the Exalted says:
"Indeed We sent down wealth to establish prayer and to give zakat. And if the son of Adam had a valley of wealth, he would seek a second to it; and if he had a second, he would seek a third. And nothing fills the belly of the son of Adam except dust."

So He informed us that He sent down wealth to be used for the establishment of His right through prayer, and for the fulfilment of His servants' rights through zakat, not for enjoyment and pleasure as cattle eat. When wealth exceeds that, or departs from these two purposes, then the aim and wisdom for which it was sent down becomes dust, and dust is more fitting for it. Thus it and the belly it fills return to the material of dust from which they were created. The belly was created to hold faith, knowledge, and wisdom. It was created to be a vessel for knowing its Lord and Creator, believing in Him, loving Him, and remembering Him. Wealth was sent down to help it accomplish this. But the one ignorant of Allah, of His command, of His oneness, and of His names and attributes, leaves his belly empty of what it was created for, and fills it with love of fleeting, perishing wealth, which departs from its owner or he from it, and with gathering and multiplying it. Yet despite this, it is never filled. Rather, he grows in poverty and greed until his belly is filled with the dust from which he was created. Then he returns to his dust-material, from which he and his wealth were created. His material was not completed by filling his belly with knowledge and faith, through which lie his perfection, success, and happiness in this life and the Hereafter. Wealth, if it does not benefit its owner, will certainly harm him. The same applies to knowledge, dominion, and power. All of that, if it does not benefit him, harms him. These things are means to ends, employed for good or for evil. If they are emptied of being used as means to praiseworthy aims and ends, they are used as means to their opposites.

So the most profitable of people is the one who makes these into means to Allah and the Last Abode. That is what benefits him in this life and the Hereafter. And the greatest loser is the one who uses them as means to his desires, to attaining his lusts and immediate aims, so he loses both this world and the Hereafter. This person did not make the means into ends. Had he made them ends, he would still be a loser, but he made them means to the opposite of what they were created for. He is like someone who uses the causes of pleasure as a means to the greatest pains and their remedies.

The divisions are four, with no fifth:
The first: one who neglects the means and turns away from them.
The second: one who is absorbed in them, stopping at gathering and acquiring them.
The third: one who uses them to reach what harms him and does not benefit him in this life or the Hereafter. These three are in loss.
The fourth: one who uses them to reach what benefits him in this life and the Hereafter. He is the profitable one. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment, We will pay them in full for their deeds therein, and they will not be shortchanged therein. Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter except the Fire, and what they did therein will come to nothing, and what they used to do is void.﴾

The understanding of this verse has been problematic for many people, as they understood from it that whoever has an intention for this world and its adornment faces this threat. Then they differed about its meaning. A group, including Ibn 'Abbas, said: whoever desires to hasten the world does not believe in resurrection, reward, or punishment. They said the verse concerns disbelievers specifically, according to Ibn 'Abbas's view.

Qatadah said: whoever has the world as his concern, his heedlessness, his intention, and his pursuit, Allah will reward him in this world for his good deeds, then he will arrive in the Hereafter with no good deed for which he can be rewarded. As for the believer, he is rewarded in this world for his good deeds and recompensed for them in the Hereafter.

These people said: the verse is about disbelievers, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter except the Fire, and what they did therein will come to nothing, and what they used to do is void.﴾ They said: the believer is one who desires both the world and the Hereafter. As for one whose intention is confined to the world, he is not a believer.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, in the narration of Abu Salih from him, said: it was revealed concerning the People of the Qibla (Muslims).

Mujahid said: they are the people of riya' (showing off).

Ad-Dahhak said: whoever does a righteous deed among the believers without piety, his reward for that deed is hastened to him in this world.

Al-Farra' chose this view and said: whoever among the People of the Qibla intends by his deed the reward of this world, his reward is hastened to him and is not diminished.

This view is more likely correct. The meaning of the verse according to it is: whoever intends by his deed the life of this world and its adornment, and such a person cannot be a believer at all. An disobedient person and a sinner, however greatly he may engage in disobedience and sin, is nonetheless moved by something to perform acts of righteousness for Allah, so he intends by these acts of righteousness the face of Allah, even if he also commits acts of disobedience.

As for one who does not intend by his deed the face of Allah, but intends only this world and its adornment, such a person does not enter the circle of the people of faith. This is what Mu'awiyah understood from the verse, and he cited it as evidence for the hadith of Abu Hurairah which Muslim related in his Sahih, about the three who will be the first whom the Fire is kindled for on the Day of Resurrection: the reciter who recited the Qur'an so that it would be said, "So-and-so is a reciter"; the giver who spent his wealth so that it would be said, "So-and-so is generous"; and the warrior who was killed in jihad so that it would be said, "He is brave."

Just as the best of Allah's creation are the prophets, the truthful ones, the martyrs, and the righteous, the worst of creation are those who imitate them without being among them. Whoever imitates the people of truth and sincerity while being a show-off is like one who imitates the prophets while being a liar.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya said: Muhammad ibn Idris related to me, he said: 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Salih informed me, he said: Qatan ibn al-Habbab related to us from 'Abd al-Warith, from Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:
"When the Day of Resurrection comes, my nation will be divided into three groups. One group worships Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for the sake of the world. Another group worships for show and reputation. And another group worships Him for His face and for His abode. Then He will say to those who worshipped Him for the world: 'By My might, My majesty, and My station, what did you intend by your worship?' They will say: 'By Your might, Your majesty, and Your station, the world.' He will say: 'I have not accepted anything of that. Take them to the Fire.' He will say to those who worshipped for show and reputation: 'By My might, My majesty, and My station, what did you intend by your worship?' They will say: 'By Your might, Your majesty, and Your station, for show and reputation.' He will say: 'I have not accepted anything of that. Take them to the Fire.' And He will say to those who worshipped Him for His face and His abode: 'By My might, My majesty, and My station, what did you intend by your worship?' They will say: 'By Your might, Your majesty, Your face, and Your abode.' He will say: 'You have spoken the truth. Take them to Paradise.'"

This is a hadith that needs no isnad, as the Qur'an and the Sunnah bear witness to its truth. The Qur'anic verse supports this view in His saying: ﴿We will pay them in full for their deeds therein﴾. This applies to people who had deeds in which they did not intend the face of Allah, but intended only the world, and for it they performed them. Allah paid them the reward of their deeds in this world without diminution, and they came to the Hereafter with no deed for which they deserve reward. This does not happen from one who believes in the Hereafter, except as an occasional lapse, as major sins occur from him, which he repents from and returns to tawhid (the oneness of God).

Ibn al-Anbari said: according to this view, the meaning concerns people among the Muslims who do good deeds so their worldly affairs will be set right, without reflecting on the Hereafter and what they will return to. These will be given the reward of their good deeds in this world. When the Hereafter comes, their recompense for them is the Fire, if they did not intend by them the face of Allah and did not seek His reward and recompense.

Then the proponent of this view raised a question against themselves. They said: if it is said that the second verse according to this view requires the eternal abiding of the believer who intends the world by his deed in the Fire?

They answered it by saying that the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that whoever does show-off in his deed and does not seek by it the reward of the Hereafter, but whose intention is the world, Allah will nullify his faith at the time of his muwafah (death in a state of faith), so he will not meet his Lord with faith. They said: this is indicated by His saying: ﴿And what they did therein came to nothing, and what they used to do is void.﴾ This encompasses both the root of faith and its branches.

Another group answered that the verse does not require eternal everlasting abiding in the Fire. It only requires that what they deserve in the Hereafter is the Fire, and that they have no righteous deed by which they hope for salvation. So if one of them has with him the pillar of tawhid, he will be brought out of the Fire along with those who come out among the major sinners who are monotheists. This is the answer of Ibn al-Anbari and others.

The verse, praise be to Allah, presents no difficulty. Allah, glorified be He, mentioned the recompense of whoever intends by his deed the life of this world and its adornment, which is the Fire, and He informed us that his deed is annulled and void. So if what he would be saved by is annulled and voided, nothing remains with him that could save him. If, however, he has faith that he did not intend for the world and its adornment, but intended by it Allah and the Last Abode, then this faith is not included in the deed that was annulled and voided, and his faith saves him from eternal abiding in the Fire, even if he enters it due to the annulment of his deed, by which the absolute salvation would have come. Faith is of two kinds: a faith that prevents entry into the Fire, which is the faith that motivates the deeds to be for Allah, seeking His face and His reward; and a faith that prevents eternal abiding in the Fire, if the show-off has some of it with him, and otherwise he would be among the people of eternal abiding. So this verse has the same ruling as its counterparts among the verses of threat. And success is from Allah. The verse is: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We will increase for him his tilth; and whoever desires the tilth of this world, We will give him from it, but he will have no share in the Hereafter.﴾

Among them is His saying: ﴿Whoever desires the hasty (life), We hasten for him therein what We will, for whomever We wish. Then We have prepared for him Hell, which he will enter, reproached and banished.﴾

These are three places in the Qur'an, some of which resemble and confirm one another, and they converge on one meaning: whoever has the world as his aim, and works for it with his utmost effort, will have no share in the Hereafter. Whoever has the Hereafter as his aim, and works for it, and it is the goal of his striving, it will be his.

It remains to be said: what is the ruling for one who desires both the world and the Hereafter? He falls under the ruling of both intentions. By which of them will he be judged? Here the problem arose, and some exegetes thought the verse concerns the disbeliever, since he is the one who desires the world rather than the Hereafter. But this is not necessarily true, either in its general application or in its converse. Some disbelievers may desire the Hereafter, and some Muslims may have no aim but the world. Allah, the Exalted, has tied happiness to the desire for the Hereafter and wretchedness to the desire for the world. So when the two intentions are separate, their consequence and requirement are separate. If they combine, their combined ruling is that of the combination of righteousness and wickedness, obedience and disobedience, faith and polytheism in one servant. Allah the Exalted said to the best of creation after the messengers: ﴿Among you are those who desire the world, and among you are those who desire the Hereafter.﴾ This address was to those who witnessed the battle with him, and among them there were no hypocrites. This is why 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I did not realize that any of the companions of the Messenger of Allah desired the world until the Day of Uhud, when this verse was revealed."

Those referred to in this verse were those who abandoned their post, which the Messenger of Allah had commanded them to guard. They were among the best of the Muslims, but this was a passing intention that led them to leave the post and turn to gathering spoils, unlike one whose intention in his deed was the world and its immediate benefit. This intention is one color, and the intention of these people is another color.

Here there is a matter that must be pointed out: it is impossible for one to desire the world and its immediate benefit through acts of righteousness, without also desiring the Hereafter, while believing in Allah and His Messenger and in meeting Him, ever. For faith in Allah and the Last Day necessitates that the servant desire the mercy of Allah and the Hereafter through his deeds. Wherever his intention through them is the world, this never combines with faith. And even if knowledge and acknowledgment combine with it, faith lies beyond that. Acknowledgment and knowledge are present in those whom Allah, glorified be He, has testified to be disbelievers despite this knowledge, such as Pharaoh, Thamud, and the Jews who witnessed the Messenger of Allah and recognized him as they recognized their own sons. They are among the greatest disbelievers in the world, desiring the world and its immediate benefit through deeds, which may combine with this knowledge and awareness. But the faith that lies beyond it necessarily requires that its possessor desire, through his deeds, Allah and the Last Abode. And Allah is the One whose help is sought.

(Section)
The point is that He, glorified be He, made wealth and poverty a trial and test of gratitude and patience, of truthfulness and lying, of sincerity and polytheism.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That He may test you in what He has given you.﴾ And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Do people think that they will be left alone because they say, "We believe," and they will not be tested? We certainly tested those before them, and Allah will surely know those who are truthful, and He will surely know the liars.﴾ And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, your wealth and your children are a trial, and with Allah is a great reward.﴾

So He made the world a fleeting possession and a deceptive enjoyment, and He made the Hereafter an abode of recompense and reward. He surrounded the world with desires and adorned it with them, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Adorned for people is the love of desires: women, children, heaped-up piles of gold and silver, branded horses, cattle, and tilth. That is the enjoyment of the life of this world, but with Allah is the best return.﴾

So He informed us that this which He adorned the world with, of its pleasures and desires, is the ultimate object of the hopes of its seekers and its preferrers over the Hereafter. It consists of seven things: women, who are the greatest of its adornments and desires, and the greatest of its trials; children, through whom a man's perfection, pride, generosity, and honor come; gold and silver, which are the material of desires in all their kinds and varieties; branded horses, which are the honor, pride, and fortresses of their owners, and the means of subduing their enemies in pursuit and in flight; cattle, from which come their mounts, food, clothing, furnishings, goods, and other benefits; and tilth, which is the material of their sustenance, the sustenance of their livestock and animals, their fruit, their medicines, and more.

Then He informed us that all of this is the enjoyment of the life of this world. Then He stirred His servants' longing for the enjoyment of the Hereafter and informed them that it is better than this enjoyment and more lasting. He said: ﴿Say: "Shall I inform you of something better than that? For those who are mindful of Allah, with their Lord are gardens beneath which rivers flow, wherein they abide forever, and pure spouses, and approval from Allah." And Allah is All-Seeing of His servants.﴾

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 1, verse 2 (part 14 of 14):

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned who deserves this enjoyment and who its people are, those who are most entitled to it, saying: ﴿Those who say, "Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us our sins and protect us from the punishment of the Fire," the patient, the truthful, the obedient, the ones who spend, and those who seek forgiveness in the hours before dawn﴾. He informed us that what He has prepared for His righteous friends of the enjoyment of the Hereafter is better than the enjoyment of this world. It has two kinds: a reward they enjoy, and something greater than it, which is His pleasure with them. The Exalted said: ﴿Know that the life of this world is only play and amusement, adornment and boasting among you, and competition in wealth and children, like a rain whose plants please the disbelievers, then it dries up and you see it turning yellow, then it becomes debris﴾. He informed us about the reality of this world through what He made visible to those of insight. It is play and diversion, by which souls are distracted and bodies are amused. Play and amusement have no real substance. They are a preoccupation for the soul and a waste of time, by which the ignorant pass their time, so it goes to waste over nothing. Then He informed us that it is an adornment, made attractive to the eyes and the souls. The eyes and souls are drawn to it through approval and love. If hearts truly knew its reality, its end and its destination, they would hate it and would prefer the Hereafter over it, and would not prefer it over the lasting, everlasting Hereafter, which is better and more enduring.

The Imam said: Wakī' narrated to us, al-Mas'ūdī narrated to us, from 'Amr ibn Murrah, from Ibrāhīm, from 'Alqamah, from 'Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet, who said:
"What have I to do with this world? My likeness and the likeness of this world is that of a rider who rested in the shade of a tree on a summer day, then departed and left it."

In Jami' al-Tirmidhi (the collection of al-Tirmidhi), from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If this world were worth the wing of a mosquito in the sight of Allah, He would not have given a disbeliever a drink of water from it." al-Tirmidhi said: This is a sound hadith.

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of al-Mustawrid ibn Shaddād, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The likeness of this world compared to the Hereafter is nothing but that of one of you dipping his finger into the sea, so let him look at what it returns with." And he pointed with the index finger.

In al-Tirmidhi, from his hadith, he said: "I was with the group of people who stopped with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) beside a dead young goat. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Do you see this, that it was worthless to its people, so that they threw it away?' They said: 'And because of its worthlessness they threw it away, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'The world is more worthless to Allah than this is to its people.'" In al-Tirmidhi also, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The world is cursed, and cursed is what is in it, except the remembrance of Allah and what accompanies it, and a scholar or a student." The two hadiths are good.

Imam Ahmad said: Haythām ibn Khārijah narrated to us, Ismā'īl ibn 'Ayyāsh informed us, from 'Abd Allah ibn Dīnār al-Nahrānī, who said: 'Īsā (peace be upon him) said to the disciples (al-hawāriyyūn): "Truly I tell you, the sweetness of this world is the bitterness of the Hereafter, and the bitterness of this world is the sweetness of the Hereafter. Truly, the servants of Allah are not those who live in luxury. Truly I tell you, the most evil of you in deed is the scholar who loves this world and prefers it over the Hereafter. If he could, he would make all people like himself in his work."

Ahmad also said: Yahyā ibn Isḥāq narrated to us, who said: Sa'īd ibn 'Abd al-'Azīz informed me, from Makhūl, who said: 'Īsā ibn Maryam (peace be upon him) said: "O company of the disciples, which of you can build a house on the waves of the sea?" They said: "O Spirit of Allah, who is able to do that?" He said: "Beware of this world, do not take it as a dwelling place."

In the Kitāb al-Zuhd (The Book of Asceticism) of Ahmad, that 'Īsā ibn Maryam (peace be upon him) used to say: "Truly I tell you, eating bread, drinking sweet water, and sleeping on rubbish heaps with the dogs is a lot for one who wants to inherit Paradise."

In the Musnad, from him (i.e., the Prophet (ﷺ)): "Allah has struck the food of the son of Adam as a likeness for this world. When it is mixed with its saliva and its salt, let him see what it turns into."

Section: Then He, glorified is He, informed us about it, that some of us boast to others with it, so one seeks it in order to boast over his companion. This is the state of everyone who seeks something for boasting, whether wealth, status, strength, knowledge, or asceticism. Boasting is of two kinds: blameworthy and praiseworthy. The blameworthy is the boasting of the people of this world with it. The praiseworthy is that one seeks to boast in the Hereafter. This is of the kind of competition (munafasah, the eager striving for something precious) that is commanded, which is that a man begrudges something to another and is jealous that it be attained without him, and refuses it and protects his pride from it. It is said: "I begrudged him the thing (nafistu 'alayhi al-shay'), I begrudge it with begrudging (nafāsah), when you withhold it and do not want it to come to him without you." Mutanāfasah (competing) is a reciprocal form from this, as if each of the rivals wanted to outrun the other to it. The reality of munafasah is complete desire, hastening, and racing toward a precious thing.

(Section)
Then He informed us about it, that it leads to mutual multiplication in wealth and children, so that each one loves to outdo his kind in that, and rejoices in seeing himself more in wealth and children than others, and in being praised for that. This is among the greatest things that distract souls from Allah and the Last Abode, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Rivalry in increase distracts you until you visit the graves. No! You will soon know. Then no! You will soon know﴾.

Multiplication (takāthur) occurs in everything. Whoever is preoccupied and distracted by multiplication in any matter from Allah and the Last Abode falls under the ruling of this verse. Some people are distracted by multiplication in wealth, some by multiplication in status or knowledge, and they gather it for multiplication and boasting. This is worse in state before Allah than the one who multiplies by wealth and status, because he has made the means of the Hereafter serve the world, while the owner of wealth and status has used the means of the world for it and multiplied by its means.

Section: Then He, glorified is He, informed us about the end of this world and its reality, that it is like rain whose plants please the disbelievers. The correct view, Allah willing, is that "the disbelievers" are disbelievers in Allah. That is the custom of the Qur'an, since they are mentioned with this description in every place. If He had intended the farmers, He would have mentioned them by the name by which they are known, as He mentioned them in His saying "pleases the farmers." He specified the disbelievers with it because they are most pleased with this world, for it is their abode, for which they work and toil. So they are most pleased with its adornment and what is in it, more than the believers are.

Then He mentioned the outcome of this plant, which is its yellowing and drying. This is the end of this world and its destination, even if a servant were to possess it from beginning to end. Its finish is that. When the Hereafter comes, the world is transformed and turned into severe punishment or forgiveness from Allah and good reward and recompense, as 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib said: "This world is an abode of truth for one who speaks truly of it, an abode of well-being for one who understands its purity, and a place of seeking success for one who is safe in it. It is the mosques of the prophets of Allah, the descent place of His revelation, the prayer place of His angels, and the marketplace of His friends. In it they acquired mercy, and in it they profited well-being. So who would blame it, when it has announced its children and described itself and its people? It has displayed itself through its trials and aroused desire for its joy through its happiness, as a warning, an admonition, and an encouragement. A people blamed it on the morning of regret, and others praised it, for it reminded them and they remembered, and it admonished them and they were admonished. O you who blame the world, deceived by its deception, when did it ask you to blame it? Or when did it deceive you? Is it by the dwellings of your fathers in the dust, or by the resting places of your mothers in affliction? How many inheritors have you seen? How many sick have you treated with your hands, seeking for them healing and asking doctors for a cure, yet your intercession did not benefit them and your effort did not help them? The world was displayed to you on the day of his fall, your fall, and his resting place, your resting place. Then he turned to the graves and said: 'O people of strangeness, O people of the grave! As for the houses, they were occupied. As for the wealth, it was divided. As for the wives, they were married. This is the news of what we have, so tell us the news of what you have.' Then he turned to us and said: 'If they were allowed, they would have told you that the best provision is piety.'"
