Thus He attributed the path to the companions who travel it, and they are those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour, so that the seeker of guidance and of treading the path may be relieved of the loneliness of being singled out from the people of his time and his kind, and so that he may know that his companion on this path is those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour. Thus he will not be concerned by the opposition of those who turn away from it, for they are the lesser in rank, even if they are the greater in number, as some of the early generations said: "Keep to the path of truth, and do not feel lonely for the fewness of those who travel it; beware of the path of falsehood, and do not be deceived by the multitude of those who perish." Whenever you feel lonely in your solitude, look to the companions who have gone ahead, eagerly strive to catch up with them, and lower your gaze from all others, for they will not avail you anything against Allah. And if they call out to you on your journey, do not turn toward them, for if you turn toward them they will seize you and hinder you.

I have given two examples for this, so let them be in your mind:

The first example: a man leaves his house for prayer, wanting nothing but that. A devil of mankind meets him on his way and throws at him words that hurt him, so he stops and responds, and they grapple. Perhaps the devil of mankind is stronger than him and overcomes him, preventing him from reaching the mosque until the prayer has passed him by. Or perhaps the man is stronger than the devil of mankind, but he becomes occupied with quarrelling with him, and so misses the first row and full attendance at the congregation. If he turns toward him, he makes him covet himself, and perhaps his resolve weakens. If he has knowledge and understanding, he increases his effort and his running in proportion to his turning or more. But if he turns away from him and occupies himself with what he is intent upon, fearing the loss of the prayer or its time, his enemy will not reach from him what he wishes.

The second example: the gazelle is swifter in running than the dog, but when it senses the dog it turns toward it, and its running weakens, so the dog overtakes it and seizes it.

The purpose: in mentioning this companion there is that which removes the loneliness of being alone, and urges one on in walking and in striving to catch up with them.

This is one of the benefits in the qunut supplication: "O Allah, guide me among those whom You have guided." That is, admit me into this company, and make me a companion to them and with them.

The second benefit: it is a means of seeking Allah's nearness through His blessings and His kindness to those upon whom He has bestowed guidance. That is: You have bestowed guidance upon those whom You guided, and that was a blessing from You; so grant me a share of this blessing, and make me one of these favoured ones. It is thus a seeking of nearness to Allah through His kindness.

The third benefit: as the petitioner says to the generous one: "Give to me among those to whom you have given, teach me among those whom you have taught, and be kind to me among those whom you have embraced with your kindness."

[Section: Soundness of understanding is a blessing]

Soundness of understanding and goodness of intention are among the greatest blessings which Allah bestows upon His servant. Indeed, no servant is given any gift after Islam better or more exalted than these two. Rather, they are the two legs of Islam and its foundation, and by them the servant is safe on the path of those who have earned anger, whose intention has been corrupted, and the path of those who have gone astray, whose understandings have been corrupted; and by them he becomes one of those upon whom favour is bestowed, whose understandings and intentions are good. They are the people of the straight path, whom we were commanded to ask Allah to guide us to in every prayer. Soundness of understanding is a light which Allah casts into the heart of the servant, by which he distinguishes between the correct and the corrupt, the truth and falsehood, guidance and misguidance, error and rectitude. It is supported by goodness of intention, seeking the truth, fearing the Lord in private and in public, and it cuts off at its root the following of desire, preferring this world, seeking the praise of creatures, and abandoning piety.

[Section: Explaining that al-Fatiha includes a refutation of the Rafidah]

This is from His words ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ to the end of it.

The way in which it includes the refutation of their view is that He, glorified is He, divided people into three categories: those upon whom favour is bestowed, who are the people of the straight path, those who knew the truth and followed it; those who have earned anger, who knew the truth and rejected it; and those who went astray, who were ignorant of it and so missed it.

Thus whoever has greater knowledge of the truth and follows it more is more worthy of the straight path.

There is no doubt that the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), may Allah be pleased with them, are more worthy of this description than the Rafidah. For it is impossible that the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), may Allah be pleased with them, were ignorant of the truth while the Rafidah knew it, or that they rejected it while the Rafidah held fast to it.

Then we see the traces of both groups indicate the people of truth among them. We see that the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) opened the lands of disbelief and turned them into lands of Islam, and opened hearts with the Qur'an, knowledge and guidance. Their traces indicate that they are the people of the straight path. We see the Rafidah in the opposite state in every time and place, for never has an enemy risen against the Muslims from others except that they were helpers to it against Islam. How much calamity have they brought upon Islam and its people? Did the swords of the idolatrous polytheists of Hulagu's army and his kin of the Tatars do their havoc except from beneath their leadership? Were the mosques not left desolate, the Qur'ans not burned, the leaders of the Muslims, their scholars, their worshippers and their caliph not slain, except through them and because of them? Their support of the polytheists and the Christians is known to the elite and the common folk, and their effects upon the religion are known.

So which of the two groups is more worthy of the straight path? And which of them is more worthy of anger and misguidance, if you know? For this reason the early generations interpreted the straight path and its people as Abu Bakr and Umar and the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), may Allah be pleased with them; and it is as they interpreted it, for it is their path, which they walked upon, and it is the very path of their Prophet. They are those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour, and against whose enemies He was angry, and He ruled that their enemies were in error. Abu al-'Aliyah Rafi' al-Riyahi and al-Hasan al-Basri, who are among the greatest of the Successors, said:

"The straight path is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his two companions."

Abu al-'Aliyah also said regarding His words "the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour": "They are the family of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Abu Bakr and Umar."

This is true, for his family and Abu Bakr and Umar are on one path; there is no disagreement among them, their mutual loyalty to one another, their praise of the two of them, their fighting against whomever they fought, and their making peace with whomever they made peace with, are known to the Ummah, elite and common. Zayd ibn Aslam said: "Those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour are the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr and Umar."

There is no doubt that those upon whom favour is bestowed are his followers, and those who have earned anger are those who depart from following him. The most obedient and most following of the Ummah to him are his companions and the people of his household, and the most following of the Companions to him, his hearing and his sight, are Abu Bakr and Umar. The most opposed of the Ummah to him are the Rafidah, and their opposition to him is known to all the sects of the Ummah. For this reason they hate the Sunnah and its people, and they are hostile to it and to its people. They are the enemies of his Sunnah (ﷺ) and of his household. Are his followers from among his descendants the ones who inherit his legacy more fully? Rather, they are truly his heirs.

It has become clear that the straight path is the way of his companions and followers, and the way of those who have earned anger and misguidance is the way of the Rafidah.

By this same path the Kharijites are refuted, for their hostility toward the Companions is well known.

(An excellent section)

Abu al-Qasim al-Rummani, the Ustadh, related a narration from Yunus that he permitted the government (i'mal) of ﴿lakin﴾ even when it is lightened (takhfif), and he found this narration strange.

Know that ﴿lakin﴾ cannot be a conjunction (harf 'atf) when the wa' is attached to it, for two conjunctive particles cannot be combined. So whenever you see one of the conjunctive particles with the wa', the wa' is the conjunctive one, not it. Among these is (imma): when you say "imma Zayd wa-imma 'Amr." Likewise (la): when you say "ma qama Zayd wa-la 'Amr," and the ﴿la﴾ is brought in to emphasise the negation, and lest one suppose that the wa' is inclusive and that you negated their standing at one time. And ﴿la﴾ is not conjunctive except after an affirmation and another condition, namely that the speech before it implies, by the implication of the address, the negation of the verb from what follows it, as in your saying: "A man came to me, not a woman," and "a learned man, not an ignorant man."

If you said "I passed by a man, not Zayd," it would not be permitted; likewise "I passed by a man, not intelligent," because there is nothing in the implication of the speech that negates the verb from the second, and ﴿la﴾ only enters to emphasise a negation. If you intend that meaning, you bring the word (ghayr), so you say "I passed by a man other than Zayd" and "a man not learned."

And you do not say "by a man other than a woman," nor "by a tall man other than short," because the implication of the address already suffices you against the negation implicit in ghayr, and that meaning is indicated by the implication, so that you say "by a tall man, not short."

As for when they are two definite nouns, such as "I passed by Zayd, not 'Amr," it is permissible here to use ghayr, because the proper noun is fixed and has no implication of address according to the usuli scholars, unlike derived nouns and what follows their pattern, such as "rajul" (man), which is equivalent to your saying "dhakar" (male). Therefore its implication indicates the transfer of the report away from the woman. It is also permissible to say "I passed by Zayd, not 'Amr," because it is a noun specific to a person, and as though, when you singled him out by mention, you negated the passing from 'Amr, then you emphasised that negation with la. But a negated statement is not conjoined to with la, because your negating the verb from Zayd when you say "ma qama Zayd" is not understood to negate it from 'Amr, so it is emphasised with la.

If you say: emphasise by it the preceding negation, it is said to you: then what would be the i'rab of 'Amr, which is a single noun, and no conjunctive particle has entered upon it to join it to what precedes? This is not permitted, unless you make it a subject (mubtada') and bring a predicate, so you say "ma qama Zayd wa-la 'Amr, wa-huwa al-qa'im" ("Zayd did not stand, nor did 'Amr; and he is the standing one").

As for if you intend to share them in the negation, there must be the wa' either alone or with la, so the wa' is not conjunctive when la is with it.

As for His words: ﴿ghayri al-maghdubi 'alayhim wa-la al-dallin﴾, the meaning of negation is present in ghayr.

If it is said: why then did He not say: ﴿la al-maghdubi 'alayhim wa-la al-dallin﴾?

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 1, verse 7 (part 4 of 8):

It has been said: the mention [of "those upon whom You have bestowed favour"] is an explanation of the superfluous, and a clarification to negate the attributes of going astray and of incurring wrath from them, and that they are the ones on whom He bestowed prophethood and guidance, and no others. Had He said, "Not those who have incurred wrath, nor those who have gone astray," this would have been nothing but an emphasis on negating the attribution of the path to those who incurred wrath, just as you say, "This is the servant of Zayd, not of 'Amr," emphasising the negation of attribution from 'Amr. This differs from your saying, "This is the servant of the jurist, not the sinner nor the wicked," as though you had combined the attribution of the servant to the jurist and not to others, which is the negation of a blameworthy attribute from the jurist. Understand this.

If it is asked: what did "lā" emphasise, such that the "wāw" was introduced before it, when you have said that it does not emphasise a previously negated item, but rather emphasises an implied element indicated by the restriction of an affirmative verb to a particular attribute, as when you say, "A learned man came to me, not an ignorant one"?

The answer: when you say "Zayd did not come to me," the sentence does not indicate the negation of coming from 'Amr, as has been explained. But when you join with "wāw," the sentence indicates that the act is negated from 'Amr as it was negated from the first, since the "wāw" takes the place of repeating the negative particle. Thus "lā" enters to emphasise the negation of the second.

(A wonderful benefit)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾.

In this there are twenty questions:

The first: What is the benefit of the substitution (badal) in supplication, when the one supplicating is addressing One who has no need of clarification? The purpose of the substitution is to clarify the first noun.

The second: What is the benefit of defining ﴿the path, the straight﴾ with the definite article? Why was it not stated merely with the word without it, as He said: ﴿And indeed you guide to a straight path﴾?

The third: What is the meaning of ﴿the path (al-ṣirāṭ)﴾, from what is it derived, why does it follow the pattern fiʿāl, why is it mentioned in most places in the Noble Qur'an with this word, and in Surat al-Aḥqāf it is mentioned with the word "road (ṭarīq)," as He said: ﴿He guides to the truth and to a straight road﴾?

The fourth: What is the wisdom in its being attributed to His saying, ﴿those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾, in this wording, and not naming them specifically, so that He would say "the path of the prophets and the truthful"? Why did He turn to the ambiguous wording rather than the explicit?

The fifth: What is the wisdom in expressing them with the phrase "those who" (alladhīna) together with its relative clause, rather than saying "the favoured (al-munʿam ʿalayhim)," which is shorter, as in ﴿those who have incurred wrath (al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim)﴾? And what is the difference?

The sixth: Why did He distinguish between "the favoured" and "those who have incurred wrath," saying of the people of favour "those upon whom You have bestowed favour," and of the people of wrath "those who have incurred wrath," with the agent deleted?

The seventh: Why did He say ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, making the verb transitive by itself without "to" (ilā), as He said, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed you guide to a straight path﴾, and He said: ﴿And We chose them and guided them to a straight path﴾?

The eighth: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have incurred wrath﴾ implies that His favour is specific to the first group, not to those who incurred wrath nor those who went astray. This is an argument for those who hold that there is no favour from Him upon an unbeliever. Is this a sound inference or not?

The ninth: It may be asked, why did He describe them with the word "other than (ghayr)," and why did He not say "not those who have incurred wrath," as He said "nor those who have gone astray"? This is like your saying, "I passed by Zayd, not 'Amr," and "by the intelligent, not the fool."

The tenth: How is "other than (ghayr)" used as an adjective of a definite noun, when it does not become definite by being in construct, and the position is not that of an appositive clarifier (ʿaṭf bayān), since that is for proper nouns, and there is no place for that, since in the case of substitution what is intended is the second and the first is a preparation, while in the case of adjectives what is intended is the first and the second is a clarification? This is the nature of this position, for the purpose is to mention those favoured and to describe them by their difference from the meaning of wrath and going astray.

The eleventh: If that is established in the case of substitution, then "the straight path" is the thing intended to be stated about, and there is no intention of discarding it. How then did "the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour" come as a substitute for it, and what is the benefit of the substitution here?

The twelfth: It is established in the hadith narrated by al-Tirmidhī, Imam Aḥmad and Ibn Abī Ḥātim: "The interpretation of those who incurred wrath as the Jews, and of those who went astray as the Christians," is good. What is the rationale of this division and restriction, when each of the two groups is both astray and under wrath?

The thirteenth: Why did He place "those who have incurred wrath" before "those who have gone astray" in the wording?

The fourteenth: Why did He use for the people of wrath the passive participle derived from the verb, and not for the people of straying, so that it would be said "al-muḍillīn (those who lead astray)," but instead used for them the active participle derived from a verb?

The fifteenth: What is the benefit of the conjunction with "lā" here? If it had been said "those who have incurred wrath and those who have gone astray," the sentence would not have been disturbed, and it would have been more concise?

The sixteenth: Since it is conjoined with it, then conjunction with "lā" comes with "wāw" after a negation, as in "Zayd did not stand, nor 'Amr," and as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak, nor upon the sick, nor upon those who find nothing to spend, when they are sincere…﴾ up to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿nor upon those who, when they came to you that you might mount them…﴾. But without "wāw," its basis is affirmation, as in "I passed by Zayd, not 'Amr"?

The seventeenth: Is the guidance here the guidance of instruction and clarification, or the guidance of enabling and inspiration?

The eighteenth: Every believer is commanded with this supplication with an obligatory command that no one else can fulfil in his place, and it is indispensable. This is only what we ask in prayer after having been guided. So what is the point of asking for something already achieved, and how can one seek to attain what has already been attained?

The nineteenth: What is the benefit of using the plural pronoun in "guide us," when the supplicant asks his Lord for himself, both in prayer and outside it, and the plural pronoun is not fitting for him? For this reason he says: "My Lord, forgive me, have mercy on me, and turn towards me"?

The twentieth: What is the reality of ﴿the straight path﴾ that the servant conceives of at the time of his asking?

These are four questions whose proper place was to come first, but the discussion has been drawn to them after the arrangement of the sixteen questions.

The answer, by God's help and His teaching: no one among His servants has knowledge except what He has taught them, and no strength except by His assistance.

(The benefit of the substitution in supplication)

This verse came in the context of teaching the servants. The right of the supplicant is that, when reciting it, he should be conscious of what he must believe, of what faith is not complete without. For supplication is the marrow of worship, and marrow exists only within bone, and bone within flesh and blood. Therefore, when it is obligatory to bring forward the articles of faith at the time of supplication, the request must be mixed with praise. For this reason the wording of the request for guidance and the desire for it came mingled with good, as an explicit declaration by the supplicant of his belief and as a means by which he seeks nearness to his Lord through that sound belief. It is as though he approaches Him through his faith and his conviction that the path of truth is the straight path, and that it is the path of those whom He has singled out with His favour and honoured with His generosity. So when he says ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, while those who oppose the truth also claim that they are on the straight path, the supplicant must hold the opposite of their view and manifest the truth that is in his soul. Therefore it was substituted and clarified for them, so that the tongue might be trained upon what the heart has believed. Within this important supplication there is an informing of two grand benefits: the first is the benefit of the statement, and the second is the benefit of what follows from the statement.

As for the benefit of the statement, it is informing about it as being straight, and that it is the straight path which He set up for the people of His favour and honour.

As for the benefit of what follows from the statement, it is the supplicant's acknowledgement of this, his affirmation of it, and his seeking nearness through this acknowledgement to his Lord. These are four benefits of the supplication for guidance to Him: the request for it, the informing about it as such, the acknowledgement and affirmation of its reality, and seeking nearness to the One being called upon through this affirmation. There is also a fifth benefit in it: the supplicant is commanded to do this because he needs it, and because his happiness and success are not complete without it. He is therefore commanded to reflect upon what he asks for and to conceive its meaning. Thus he is told of its attributes, so that if it is imagined in his mind and settles in his heart, his seeking for it becomes stronger, his desire for it greater, and his eagerness to continue asking for it more intense. So reflect upon these wonderful subtleties.

(Section)

As for the second question, which concerns the definiteness of "the path" with the article:

Know that when the article "al-" enters upon a described noun, it implies that it is more entitled to that attribute than others. Do you not see that your saying "he sat with a jurist (faqīh) or a scholar (ʿālim)" is not like your saying "he sat with the jurist or the scholar," nor like your saying "I ate something good (ṭayyib)" as compared with "I ate the good (al-ṭayyib)"? Do you not see the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "You are the Truth, and Your promise is the Truth, and Your word is the Truth, and the meeting with You is the Truth, and Paradise is true, and the Fire is true," which al-Bukhārī and Muslim narrated? So he did not place the article upon created nouns, and he placed it upon the name of the Lord, Exalted is He, and His promise and His speech. When you have understood this, then if He had said "guide us to a straight path," the supplicant would be seeking guidance to a straight path in an absolute sense. But that is not the intention. The intention is guidance to the specific path that God, Exalted is He, has set up for the people of His favour, and has made a way to His good pleasure and His Paradise, which is His religion, and there is no religion for Him other than it. The thing sought is therefore a specific matter, both in the external world and in the mind, not some unrestricted indefinite thing. The article here is for the known mental reference (al-ʿahd al-ʿilmī al-dhihnī): it is a request for guidance to a known secret whose knowledge has been established in the hearts, whose affirmation is held, and which is distinguished from all other paths of error. Therefore definiteness was necessary.

If it is asked: why did it come indefinite in His saying to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿And guide you to a straight path﴾, and His saying: ﴿And indeed you guide to a straight path﴾, and His saying: ﴿And We chose them and guided them to a straight path﴾, and His saying: ﴿Say: My Lord has guided me to a straight path﴾?

The answer to these instances is one answer: they are not in the context of supplication and request, but in the context of informing from God, Exalted is He, about His guidance to a straight path, and the guidance of His Messenger to it. The addressees had no prior acquaintance with it, and it was not known to them. So it did not come defined by the article of known reference, which points to something known in the mind of the addressee, established in his soul, nor was there any previously mentioned referent in speech that would make the article known to him. The article of known reference comes only in one of two situations: either it has a known referent in the mind, or a verbal mention. Since neither exists in these instances, the indefinite is the original form. This is unlike His saying "guide us to the straight path," for when it had been established among the addressees that God has a straight path to which He guided His prophets and messengers, and the Addressee being asked for guidance, the Exalted, was known to have it, the article entered upon it, and He said: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾.

Al-Suhaylī said: the saying of God, Exalted is He, ﴿And guide you to a straight path﴾ was revealed concerning the Treaty of al-Ḥudaybiyya. The Muslims had disliked that treaty and thought that the right course was the opposite. God is exalted above what they say, and His Messenger (ﷺ) knew better. So God sent down this verse to His Messenger (ﷺ). Thus He did not intend a straight path in religion, but a path in judgement, in war and in strategy. Al-Suhaylī's view, however, is weak. The saying of God, Exalted is He, ﴿And indeed you guide to a straight path﴾ means: you guide from disbelief and error to a straight path. If He had said in this context "to the straight path," it would have granted disbelief and error a portion of straightness, since the article indicates that what it enters upon is more entitled to that meaning than what is mentioned after it in speech, or what is nearer in the imagination, and nothing is more entitled to it unless there is some part of it in the latter. It is not hidden how weak and feeble these two answers are.

As for his statement that the intention of ﴿And guide you to a straight path﴾ is war and strategy, this diminishes the great virtue and the abundant portion which God bestowed upon His Messenger (ﷺ). The Prophet (ﷺ) informed that this verse was more beloved to him than the world and all that is in it. And when has God called war and strategy a straight path? Has anyone among the Salaf or the later scholars interpreted this verse in that way? Rather, the straight path is that upon which God placed guidance, and the religion of truth which He commanded him to announce, namely that God guided him to it, in His saying: ﴿Say: My Lord has guided me to a straight path﴾. Then He explained it with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a upright religion, the creed of Abraham, a ḥanīf, and he was not of the polytheists﴾. Here the word "religion (dīnan)" is in the accusative as a substitution for the prepositional phrase: meaning, He guided me to an upright religion. Can he then, in this place, say that it means war and strategy? This interpretation is utterly corrupt.

Consider what God, Glorified is He, gathered for His Messenger in the verse of victory from kinds of gifts. They are five things:

The first: the manifest victory.

The second: the forgiveness of what was before of his sins and what came after.

The third: His guidance to the straight path.

The fourth: the completion of His favour upon him.

The fifth: the granting of mighty victory.

God, Glorified is He, combined for him guidance and victory, because these two foundations are the basis of the perfection of happiness and success. Guidance is knowledge of God and His religion, and acting in accordance with His good pleasure and obedience. It is beneficial knowledge and righteous action. Victory is the complete power to carry out His religion: the proof, the clarification, the sword and the spear. Victory is by proof and clarity, subduing the hearts of those who oppose it through proof, and subduing their bodies by the hand. God, Exalted is He, often combines these two foundations, for by them the completion of the call is achieved and His religion is made to prevail over all religion, as in His saying: ﴿He it is who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth﴾, in two places: in Surat al-Tawba and in Surat al-Ṣaff. And He said: ﴿We have indeed sent Our messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them the Book and the Balance, that people may uphold justice﴾. This is guidance. Then He said: ﴿And We sent down iron, wherein is mighty violence﴾. This is victory. He mentioned the guiding Book and the victorious iron. And He said: ﴿Alif, Lām, Mīm. Allāh, there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting. He has sent down upon you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it, and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel before, as guidance for mankind, and He sent down the Criterion﴾. Here He mentioned the sending down of the guiding Book and the Criterion, which is victory that distinguishes truth from falsehood. The secret of the pairing of victory with guidance is that each of them achieves the distinction between truth and falsehood. For this reason God, Exalted is He, called what He grants His believing servants of victory "criterion (furqān)," as He said: ﴿If you have believed in God, and in what We sent down upon Our servant on the Day of the Criterion, the day the two hosts met﴾. So He mentioned the two foundations: what He sent down upon His Messenger on the Day of the Criterion, which is the Day of Badr, the day on which God distinguished between truth and falsehood by the victory of His Messenger and His religion, and the humiliation and disgrace of his enemies. From this is His saying: ﴿And We indeed gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion, and a light and a reminder for the God-fearing﴾. The Criterion was His victory for him over Pharaoh and his people; the light and the reminder were the Torah. This is the meaning of the verse. Whoever said that the "wāw" is superfluous and that "light" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state has erred, as we have shown the weakness of that in al-Amālī al-Makkiyya. So it has been shown that the verse of victory comprised the two foundations, guidance and victory, and that nothing else in it is valid at all.

As for his second answer concerning His saying: ﴿And indeed you guide to a straight path﴾, that if it were defined, it would grant disbelief and error a portion of straightness: I do not know from where he derived this understanding, despite his piercing intellect and wonderful understanding, may God have mercy on him. It is nothing but the stumble of a steed and the blunting of a sword. Do you think His saying: ﴿And We gave them both the clear Book, and guided them to the straight path﴾ implies that others have a portion of straightness, when there is no other than the paths of error? The straight path is one, and it is that to which God guided all His prophets and messengers, and it is the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour. Likewise, its definition in Surat al-Fātiḥa: can it be said that it implies that others have a portion of straightness? Rather it is said that its definition indicates that others have no portion of straightness, for the definite article is equivalent to restriction. It is as though it were said: "the one that has no straight path other than it." The understanding of this restriction from the wording is stronger than the understanding of sharing. Reflect upon this, here and in its like.

(Section)

As for the third question, which concerns the derivation of "al-ṣirāṭ":

The well-known view is that it derives from "ṣaraṭtu al-shayʾa aṣrituhu," meaning I swallowed the thing with an easy swallowing. The path was called "ṣirāṭ" because it swallows up those who traverse it. The ṣirāṭ is that which combines five attributes: it is a path that is straight, easy, travelled, wide, and leads to the intended goal. The Arabs therefore do not call a crooked road a ṣirāṭ, nor a difficult, rough one, nor a blocked one that does not lead through. Whoever reflects on the occurrences of the word ṣirāṭ in their language and usage will see this. Jarīr said:

The Commander of the Believers is upon a ṣirāṭ, when the watering-places become crooked, it is straight.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 1, verse 7 (part 5 of 8):

They formed the word al-ṣirāṭ (the path) on the pattern fiʿāl, because it envelops its traveller in the way that a sheath (ḥalq) encloses the thing that is placed in it. This pattern is common for things that enclose or cover other things, such as al-liḥāf (quilt), al-khimār (veil), al-ridāʾ (cloak), al-ghiṭāʾ (covering), al-firāsh (bedding), and al-kitāb (book), and the rest of this category. The pattern fiʿāl comes with three meanings. The first is the verbal noun (maṣdar), as in al-qitāl (fighting) and al-ḍirāb (striking). The second is the object of the action (maf‘ūl), as in al-kitāb (the written thing), al-bināʾ (the building), and al-ghirās (the planting). The third is that it denotes the instrument by which the action is performed and through which it takes place, such as al-khimār (the veil), al-ghiṭāʾ (the covering), and al-sidād (the stopper), which is what one covers, shields, or plugs with. This is a pure instrument, while the object is the thing that is veiled, covered, or stopped. Of this third category is ilāh in the sense of maʾlūh (one who is worshipped).

As for its mention with the word ṭarīq (path) specifically in Surat al-Aḥqāf, this is God's report of the speech of the believing jinn, who said to their people: ﴿Indeed, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses, confirming what came before it, guiding to the truth and to a straight path.﴾ Their expression here, using ṭarīq, carries a wonderful subtlety: they had mentioned Moses before it, and that the Book they heard confirmed what was before it of the Book of Moses and others. So it was, in it, like the report about the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in his saying to his people: ﴿I am not an innovation among the messengers﴾, meaning, I was not the first messenger sent to the people of the earth; rather, messengers from God had come before to the nations, and I was only sent confirming them with the same thing they were sent with, namely monotheism and faith. So the believing jinn said: ﴿Indeed, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses, confirming what came before it, guiding to the truth and to a straight path.﴾ That is, to a well-trodden way, upon which the messengers before him had walked, and that it is not an innovation, as He said at the beginning of this same surah. Thus eloquence and inimitability required the word ṭarīq, because it is faʿīl in the sense of maf‘ūl, that is, trodden, upon which the messengers and prophets walked before. It is therefore incumbent upon whoever believes in God's messengers and has faith in them to affirm and believe in this. Mentioning ṭarīq here is more fitting, because it is more apt for the domain of the call and for drawing attention to the necessity of following it. And God knows best. Then I saw that al-Suhaylī (d. 581 AH) had mentioned this very same meaning, so his insight matched mine.

(Section)
As for the fourth issue, namely its attachment to the general relative pronoun (alladhīna) rather than saying "the path of the prophets and messengers":
There are three benefits in this. The first: it brings knowledge to mind and alerts the intellect upon hearing it, for the basis of their being among those upon whom favour was bestowed is their being guided to this path. By it they became people of blessing. This is like how a ruling is attached to a relative clause (ṣila) rather than to a rigid noun, because the clause carries the sense of the favour, the entitlement to what the ruling is attached to by it. An example is God's saying: ﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly, for them is their reward with their Lord﴾; ﴿And he who brings the truth and confirms it, those are the righteous﴾; ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is God," and then remain steadfast, no fear will be upon them.﴾ This pattern is consistent. So using the relative pronoun with this meaning is more apt than naming a specific noun. The second: it points to the removal of blind imitation from the heart and to the sense of knowledge that whoever is guided to this path has been favoured, so the one who asks is conscious of asking for guidance and seeking God's favour upon him. The difference between this aspect and the previous one is that the first includes a statement that the people of favour are the people of being guided to it, while the second includes a request and a desire that it be from Him. The third: the verse is general across all classes of those upon whom favour is bestowed. Had he used a specific noun, the request for guidance to the path of all those upon whom favour was bestowed would not have been included. So using the general noun carries the benefit that what is asked for is guidance to all the details of the way travelled by everyone upon whom favour was bestowed, from the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. This is the most noble object of desire and the greatest thing asked for. Had the supplicant known the worth of this request, he would have made it his constant utterance and tied it to his breaths, for it encompasses every good of this world and the next. Because it has this standing, God made it obligatory upon all His servants as a repeated obligation each day and night, which nothing else can replace. From this one understands the specification of al-Fātiḥah in the prayer, and that there is no substitute that can take its place.

(Section)
As for the fifth issue, namely His saying ﴿those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ rather than "the favoured ones," as He said "those who have earned anger," its answer and the answer to the sixth issue are one, and it has several benefits. The first: this follows the familiar manner of the Noble Qur'an, in which acts of kindness, mercy, and generosity are attributed to God, the Glorified and Exalted, so the agent is mentioned and attributed to Him, and the verb is not put in the passive with them. When acts of justice, recompense, and punishment are mentioned, the agent is dropped and the verb is put in the passive, out of courtesy in address. Attributing them to God, the Exalted, is the nobler of the two categories of His actions. From this is this verse: He mentioned the favour and attributed it to Himself and did not drop its agent. When He mentioned anger, He dropped the agent and put the verb in the passive, saying: ﴿those who have earned anger﴾, and about kindness He said ﴿those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾. A parallel is the saying of Abraham the Friend, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him: ﴿Who created me, and He guides me; who feeds me and gives me drink; and when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾. He attributed creation, guidance, and the feeding and giving of drink to God, the Exalted. When he came to illness he said "when I am ill" and did not say "He made me ill," and he said "it is He who cures me." From this is God's saying, reporting the believing jinn: ﴿And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether their Lord intends for them right guidance.﴾ They attributed the intention of right guidance to the Lord and dropped the agent of the intention of evil, putting the verb in the passive. From this is the saying of al-Khiḍr, peace be upon him, about the ship: ﴿So I wished to damage it﴾, where he attributed the damage to himself, and about the two boys he said: ﴿So your Lord wished that they reach their maturity.﴾ From this is God's saying: ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of fasting to go to your wives﴾, where He dropped the agent and put the verb in the passive, and then said: ﴿And God made trade lawful and forbade usury.﴾ This is because mentioning the sexual relation (rafath) carries what makes it fitting not to couple it with an explicit agent. From this is: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine﴾, and His saying: ﴿Say: "Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you: that you associate nothing with Him, and to be good to your parents"﴾ to the end. From this, and it is more subtle and precise in meaning, is His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters﴾ to the end; then He said: ﴿And lawful to you is what is beyond that﴾. Reflect on His saying: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them﴾, how He explicitly stated the agent of forbidding in this place, and for the believers He said: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion and blood﴾.

The second benefit: the bestowal of favour through guidance requires gratitude to the One who bestows it, and the root of gratitude is remembering the benefactor and acting in obedience to Him. Part of thanking Him is to make prominent the pronoun that contains the remembrance of Him, the Exalted, which is the foundation of gratitude. In His saying ﴿those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ there is a remembrance of Him and an attribution of the favour to Him that is absent if one said "the favoured ones." So this phrase includes the two principles, gratitude and remembrance, mentioned in His saying: ﴿So remember Me, and I will remember you; and be grateful to Me, and do not deny Me﴾.

The third benefit: the favour of guidance to the path belongs to God alone, He alone is the bestower of guidance, and no one shares in His favour. His exclusive ownership of it requires that it be attributed to Him with the form of singularity, so it is said: "You have bestowed favour upon them," that is, You alone are the benefactor, the bestower of kindness, the one who grants this favour. As for anger, God, Glory be to Him, became angry with those who were not among the people of being guided to this path, and He commanded His believing servants to be hostile to them. This entails their anger against them, in agreement with their Lord's anger against them. Agreement with Him requires that one be angry with whom He is angry and be pleased with whom He is pleased, so one becomes angry in accordance with His anger and pleased in accordance with His pleasure. This is the reality of servanthood. The Jews are those with whom God is angry, so it is right for the believers to be angry with them. Thus the agent of anger was dropped and it was said "those who have earned anger." Since believers have a share in God's anger toward them, unlike favour, which belongs to Him alone, reflect on these exquisite subtleties.

The fourth benefit: those who earned anger are in the position of being turned away from, of not paying attention to them, and of confining oneself to the very attribute they have. The people of favour, however, are in the position of being pointed out, specified, and honoured by mention. Given this, the alif and lam in al-maghḍūb, though they carry the meaning of alladhīna, are not like alladhīna in explicit identification and in pointing to the specific identity of the named. When you say alladhīna faʿalū (those who did), its meaning is "the people who did." Your saying al-ḍāribūn (the strikers) and al-maḍrūbūn (the struck) does not carry what your saying alladhīna ḍarabū (those who struck) or ḍuribū carries. Reflect on this. So "those upon whom You have bestowed favour" is a pointing to their identification by name and an intention to their persons, unlike "those who have earned anger," where the aim is to warn against their attribute, to turn away from them, and not to pay attention to them. The reliance in the answers is on what has already been stated.

(Section)
The seventh issue: the verb here is transitive directly without the preposition (ilā).
Its answer is that the verb of guidance is transitive at times directly, at times with the preposition ilā, and at times with the preposition lām, and all three occur in the Qur'an. Among those transitive directly is this verse, and His saying: ﴿And guide you to a straight path﴾. Among those with ilā is His saying: ﴿And indeed you guide to a straight path﴾, and His saying: ﴿Say: "Indeed my Lord has guided me to a straight path"﴾. Among those with lām is His saying in the words of the people of Paradise: ﴿Praise be to God who guided us to this﴾, and His saying: ﴿Indeed this Qur'an guides to what is most upright﴾. The distinctions among these instances are very subtle and beyond the understanding of most scholars, but we will mention a principle that points to the distinction. It is that a verb transitive by several different prepositions must not have, with each preposition, a meaning beyond the meaning of the other preposition. This depends on the variation in the meanings of the prepositions. If the difference between the two prepositions is apparent, the distinction is apparent, as in: raghibtu ʿanhu and raghibtu fīhi (I turned away from it / I desired it), ʿadaltu ilayhi and ʿadaltu ʿanhu (I turned toward it / I turned away from it), mltu ilayhi and mltu ʿanhu (I inclined to it / I deviated from it), saʿaytu ilayhi and saʿaytu bihi (I strove toward it / I pursued it with it). If the meanings of the particles are close, the distinction is difficult, as in: qaṣadtu ilayhi and qaṣadtu lahu (I aimed at it / I intended it for him), hadaytuhu ilā kadhā and hadaytuhu li-kadhā (I guided him to such-and-such / I guided him for such-and-such). Some grammarians make one preposition equivalent to another, but the jurists of the Arabic language do not accept this method. Rather, they give the verb one meaning with the preposition and another meaning with a different one. They look at the preposition and what verbs it requires, and they make the verb transitive by it take its meaning. This is the method of the master of the craft, Sībawayh, may God have mercy on him, and the method of the skilled among his companions, who make the verb imply the meaning of another verb, not placing one preposition in place of another. This is a noble and great rule that requires insight and subtlety of mind. An example is His saying: ﴿A spring from which the servants of God drink﴾, where they make yashrabu (drink) imply the meaning of yarwā (to quench the thirst), and so it is transitive with the bāʾ that yarwā requires. This gives evidence of both verbs: one stated explicitly, and the other implied and indicated by the preposition that it requires, with utmost brevity. This is among the wonders, excellences, and perfections of the language. From this is His saying about the clouds: "They drank with the water of the sea until they were quenched, then they rose and ascended," which is better than saying "drinks from it," since that gives no indication of quenching, nor "is quenched by it," since that does not indicate drinking by its explicit meaning but only by implication. When one says yashrabu bihā, it indicates drinking by its explicit meaning and quenching, unlike with the preposition min. Reflect on this.

From this is His saying: ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation with wrongdoing, We will make him taste a painful punishment.﴾ The verb irādah (intend) is not transitive with bāʾ, but it implies the meaning of yahummu fīhi bi-kadhā (to resolve upon something in it), which is stronger than mere intention. So mentioning the bāʾ indicates that the punishment is deserved upon the intention even if it is not a firm resolve. This is a broad topic, and if we pursued it at length the discussion would be long. The two examples mentioned suffice. Once you understand this: when the verb of guidance is transitive with ilā, it implies arrival at the desired goal, so the particle of the endpoint is used. When it is transitive with lām, it implies specification with the desired thing, so the lām that indicates exclusivity and determination is used. When you say hadaytuhu li-kadhā, the meaning understood is that you mentioned it to him, made it for him, prepared it for him, and similar things. When it is transitive directly, it implies the meaning that gathers all of these, namely making known, clarifying, and inspiring. So the one who says: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ is asking God to make it known to him, to clarify it for him, to inspire it in him, and to empower him upon it, placing knowledge of it and the will to it in his heart, and the power to do it. The verb was therefore stripped of the preposition and used by itself, transitive directly, to include all these levels. Had it been transitive with a preposition, its meaning would have been fixed and specified according to the meaning of the preposition. So reflect on it, for it is among the subtleties and secrets of the language.

(Section)
As for the eighth issue: namely that He specified the people of happiness with guidance, and not others.
This is a question on which people have differed and their disputes have been long from both sides. It is whether God has a favour upon the unbeliever or not.
Those who deny it argue from this verse and from His saying: ﴿And whoever obeys God and the Messenger, those are with those upon whom God has bestowed favour, of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous, and excellent companions they are.﴾
He specified these with favour, which shows that others are not favoured. They also argue from His saying to the believing servants: ﴿And that I may complete My favour upon you﴾, and from the fact that favour is incompatible with vengeance and punishment. How is there favour upon one created for everlasting punishment?
Those who affirm it argue from His saying: ﴿And if you count the favour of God, you cannot enumerate it﴾, and His saying to the Jews: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾, which is addressed to them in their state of disbelief. They also argue from His saying in Surat al-Naḥl, in which He enumerates His general favours upon His servants from the beginning to His saying: ﴿Thus He completes His favour upon you, that you may submit. But if they turn away, then upon you is only the clear conveyance. They recognise the favour of God, then deny it, and most of them are disbelievers.﴾
This is an explicit text that admits of no alteration.
They also argue that the righteous and the wicked, the believer and the disbeliever, all live in the favour of God, and everyone acknowledges to God that he lives only in His favour. This is known by necessity to all categories of the children of Adam, except one who denies and rejects the right of God and disbelieves in His favour.
The decisive resolution of the question is that absolute favour is specific to the people of faith, and no one else shares in it, while general favour is common to all creation, the righteous and the wicked, the believer and the disbeliever. Complete absolute favour is that which is connected with eternal happiness and everlasting bliss, and this is not shared.
General favour is common and shared. So if the denier intends to negate absolute favour for the disbeliever, he is correct, and if he intends to affirm general favour, he is correct.
With this the proofs agree, the dispute is removed, and it becomes clear that each of the two groups has both error and correctness. And God is the one who grants success in what is right.
As for His saying: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾, He is reminding them of His favour upon their forefathers. This is why He enumerates it one by one: that He rescued them from the household of Pharaoh, that He split the sea for them, that He appointed forty nights for Moses, after which they went astray, then He forgave them and pardoned them, that He shaded them with clouds and sent down manna and quails for them, and other favours He enumerates for them. These were for their predecessors and forefathers, so He commanded them to remember them, in order that their remembrance of them might call them to His obedience and to belief in His messengers, and to beware of His punishment with which He punished those who did not believe in His messenger and did not submit to His religion and obedience. His favour upon their forefathers was a favour from Him upon them that demanded gratitude from them. So how do you substitute for gratitude for it your disbelief in My messenger, your denial of him, and your hostility toward him? This does not indicate that His absolute complete favour was present for them in their state of disbelief. And God knows best.

(Section)
The ninth issue: namely that He said ﴿other than those who have earned anger﴾ and did not say "not those who have earned anger."

It is said: there is no doubt that "lā" (not) is used to introduce a conjunction after an affirmative statement, as you say "Zayd came to me, not ʿAmr" and "the scholar came to me, not the ignorant man." As for *ghayr*, it is a follower of what precedes it, and it is a qualifier (ṣifa) and nothing else, as will come. Presenting the statement here in the form of a qualifier is better than presenting it in the form of a conjunction. This is only known when one knows the difference between conjunction (ʿaṭf) in this position and qualification (waṣf). So you say: if the statement were presented in the form of a conjunction and it was said, "*the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour*, not *those who have earned anger*," the use of *lā* would have amounted to no more than negating the attribution of the path to those who have earned anger, which is what conjunction requires. When you say, "The scholar came to me, not the ignorant man," the conjunction does no more than negate the coming from the ignorant man and affirm it for the scholar. But when the phrase *ghayr* is used, it is a qualifier of what precedes it, so the statement, with it, conveys a description of them with two things: first, that they are those upon whom favour was bestowed; and second, that they are not those who have earned anger. It conveys what conjunction conveys, with the added praise and commendation of them. It includes two qualities: an affirmative one, which is that they are those upon whom favour was bestowed, and a negative one, which is that they do not deserve the attribute of anger and that they are distinct from its people. For this reason, when this meaning was intended, it was used as a qualifier of "those upon whom favour was bestowed," and it was not made an accusative of exception (istithnāʾ), because with that the intended meaning of qualification would be lost. There is another benefit in it: the People of the Book, the Jews and Christians, claimed that they alone were those upon whom favour was bestowed, to the exclusion of the people of Islam. So it is as if it were said to them, "Those upon whom favour has been bestowed are other than you, not you." And it is said to the Muslims, "Those who have earned anger are other than you, not you." Therefore the use of the word *ghayr* in this context is better and more indicative of establishing the required distinction. Reflect on it.

And consider how He said "those who have earned anger" and "nor those who are astray," and did not say "the Jews and the Christians," although they are the ones described by that, in order to isolate their description with anger and error, by which they differed from those upon whom favour was bestowed and did not share in that path. For absolute favour is incompatible with anger and error, so neither the one who has earned anger nor the one who is astray can be ascribed it. Blessed is He who placed in His speech secrets that testify that it is a revelation from the Wise, the Praiseworthy.

(Section)

As for the tenth issue, which is the qualification of a definite noun (maʿrifa) by *ghayr*, while *ghayr* is not made definite by annexation (iḍāfa):

There are three views on it. The first is that *ghayr* here is a substitute (badal) and not a qualifier, and that substituting an indefinite for a definite is permissible. This view is false for three reasons.

The first: in the case of substitution, what is intended is the second term, and the first is a preparation and groundwork for it. Its purpose is what is mentioned. So the words of God Most High, "And due to God from the people is the pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to make his way to it," the intended meaning is only those who have the ability, and the mention of "the people" before them is a preparation. And your saying "Zayd pleased me, his knowledge," the admiration fell only on his knowledge, and you mentioned his owner as a preparation for mentioning it. Likewise His words, "They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it," the intended meaning is only the question about fighting in the sacred month, not about the month itself. This is very clear in partial substitution and substitution of inclusion, and it is observed in whole-from-whole substitution, which is why it is called a substitute (badal), indicating that it is the one intended. So His words, "We will surely seize by the forelock, a lying, sinning forelock," the intended meaning is: "We will surely seize by the lying, sinning forelock," and the mention of the substituted term is a preparation for it. Once this is understood, the intended meaning here is the mention of those upon whom favour was bestowed and the annexation of the path to them. Part of the completion and perfection of this intended meaning is the information that they differ from those who have earned anger. So the mention of "other than those who have earned anger" comes as a completion, a perfecting, and a confirmation of this meaning, because the people of the path whose guidance is asked are the people of favour. Their not being those who have earned anger is a confirmed attribute, and its function is that of a qualifier that clarifies and completes the qualified. This is clear.

The second: a substitute functions as an emphasis, repetition, or reiteration of the substituted term. For this reason it is treated as a repetition of the governing verb, and the intended term is the mentioned term, as already noted. So it is the first itself in essence and attribute, and it is mentioned with a different intended attribute, like His words, "Guide us to the straight path," "the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour." For this reason it is good to rely on it alone without the first, and this does not make the statement deficient. Do you not see that if you said, outside the Qur'an, "To God is the pilgrimage to the House for those who are able to make their way to it," it would be complete and correct with no flaw? And if you said in your supplication, "My Lord, guide me to the path of those whom You have favoured among Your servants," it would be correct. If that is so, then if one supposed restricting the statement to *ghayr* and what falls within its scope, the statement would be disrupted and most of its intended meaning would be lost, since the intention is the annexation of the path to those upon whom God has bestowed favour, not its annexation to "other than those who have earned anger." Rather, the word *ghayr* was used as an addition to their description and as praise of them. So reflect on it.

The third view, that *ghayr* can hardly be understood as a substitute, but only as a qualifier, an accusative of exception (istithnāʾ), or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The reason for this is that it was not established to stand independently by itself, but is only ever a follower of something else. For this reason one rarely says "a man other than Zayd came to me" or "I passed by someone other than ʿAmr." A substitute must be independent in itself, as has been shown, since it is the intended term. The subtle point of the distinction is that in substitution you intend the second term, you are directed toward it, and you have made the first a ladder and a stepping-stone to it. So it is the place of your intention and the target of your will. In the case of qualification it is otherwise: you intend the qualified thing and clarify it by its attribute. So take this subtle point as a criterion for substitution and qualification, and then weigh by it "other than those who have earned anger," whether it can be a substitute or a qualifier.

The second answer: here *ghayr* is validly used as a qualifier of a definite noun, because it is a relative construction (mawṣūl), and the relative is ambiguous and not specific, so it has a trace of indefiniteness due to its ambiguity, since it does not indicate a specific referent. So it is valid to qualify it with *ghayr*, owing to its nearness to the indefinite. This is the answer of the author of the *Kashshaf*.

If it is said: how can *ghayr* validly come as a qualifier of a definite noun when it is not made definite even when annexed to definite nouns? I say: "those upon whom You have bestowed favour" contains no specification (tawqīt), so it is like the poet's words:

*"And indeed I pass by the base man, who insults me, so I go on, and then I say, 'It does not concern me.'"*

The meaning of "it contains no specification" is that there is no fixing of one individual from another as definiteness fixes it; rather it is absolute in its class, so it functions as an indefinite. The poet's verse is cited to show that the verb is indefinite, namely "who insults me," and he has made it a qualifier of "the base man," who is definite by the article, because he is not specific, so it is in effect indefinite. Thus it was valid to describe it with an indefinite. It is as if he said, "a base man who insults me." This argument is weak, because "who insults me" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) about him and not a qualifier. Its governing verb is the verb of passing, meaning: "I pass by the base man while he is insulting me," that is, I pass by him in this state, so I overlook him and do not mind his insult.

The third answer, which is the correct one: here *ghayr* has in fact become definite by annexation. What prevents it from becoming definite is its great ambiguity or generality, since it applies to everything different from what is mentioned, so no specific referent is fixed by it. This is why it is used as a qualifier of an indefinite noun, as one says "a man other than you says such-and-such and does such-and-such," and so it qualifies an indefinite even when annexed to a definite. It is known that this ambiguity disappears when it falls between two opposites, one of which is mentioned, and then you annex it to the second, so it becomes specific by annexation and the ambiguity that prevents its definiteness by annexation disappears. As the poet said:

*"We are the sons of ʿAmr al-Hajjan al-Azhar, the noble lineage, known, not disowned."*

Do you not see that he used "not disowned" (ghayr al-munkar) as a qualifier of "lineage," just as "known" (al-maʿrūf) was used as a qualifier of it, because both are specific qualifiers? So there is no ambiguity in *ghayr* here, because its opposite is "known," which is definite, and its opposite "disowned" is distinguished and specified, like the specification of the definite noun, namely the specification of the class. So it is with His words, "the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour," for those who were favoured are other than those who have earned anger. When the first term is definite, *ghayr* becomes definite, because it is annexed to a specific, distinguished, unambiguous thing, and so it takes definiteness from it. You should be alert here to a subtle point about *ghayr* that will reveal to you its true nature: when it is definite and when it is indefinite. It is that *ghayr* is itself what it follows, and the opposite of what it is annexed to. It refers to its head in the way that a synonymous noun refers to its synonym. The definite is the explanation of the indefinite, and "those upon whom favour was bestowed are other than those who have earned anger" is the real meaning of the expression. So if its head is indefinite, it is only indefinite, even when annexed, as when you say "a man other than you did such-and-such." If its head is definite, it is only definite, as when it is said, "The virtuous, other than the evildoer, is loved and revered by people; the righteous, other than the wicked, is awe-inspiring; the just, other than the unjust, has his supplication answered." In such cases *ghayr* is only definite, and whoever claims that it is indefinite here has erred, says what has no proof, since there is no ambiguity in it at all. So reflect on it.

If it is said: the lack of its definiteness by annexation has another cause, namely that it has the meaning of a different thing, being the active participle of "to differ" (ghāyara), just as *mithl* means "like" (mumāthil) and *shibh* means "similar" (mushābih). The nouns of agency are not made definite by annexation, and neither is what takes their place. I say: the active participle is not made definite by annexation only when it is annexed to its object, as in "this is a striker of Zayd tomorrow," where the annexation is in the sense of separation. *Ghayr* does not function as an operator on what follows it in the way that an active participle governs its object. So it is not the case that annexation is in the sense of separation. Rather its annexation is a pure annexation (iḍāfa maḥḍa), like the annexation of other indefinites. Do you not see that your saying "*ghayrak*" (other than you) is equivalent to your saying "*siwāk*" (other than you), and there is no difference between them? And God knows best.

(Section)

As for the eleventh issue: what is the point of presenting the statement in His words, "Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour," in the form of a substitute, even though the first term is intended to be dropped?

The answer: the saying that the first term in a substitution is intended to be dropped is not a statement that can be taken in its absolute sense. Rather, substitution is of two kinds. One kind is that in which the first term is intended to be dropped, namely substitution of a part from a whole and substitution of inclusion, because the second term is the intended one and not the first, as already mentioned. The other kind is that in which dropping the first term is not intended, namely whole-from-whole substitution. Here the second term is in the position of emphasis, reiteration, and strengthening of the predication, along with the additional benefit that the predication gives to it beyond the first. So the benefit of the substitution is emphasis and an indication that the substituted term has the attribute of the term it replaces. When He said, "Guide us to the straight path," it is as if the mind sought knowledge of whether this path is restricted to us or whether others whom God has guided have trodden it. So He said, "the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour." This is like when you guide a man to a road he does not know, and you want to emphasize the guidance and urge him to keep to it and not leave it. You say, "This is the road that leads to your goal," and then you increase that in his mind by emphasis and reinforcement, saying, "and it is the road that people, travellers, and the people of salvation have trodden." Do you not see how your description of it as the road of those who travel and are saved adds a greater measure of value than your description of it as a road that is connected, near, easy, and straight? For souls are naturally inclined to imitation and following. So when someone to be imitated in traversing it is mentioned to them, they are reassured and enter upon it. So reflect on it.

(Section)

As for the twelfth issue: what is the basis for interpreting "those who have earned anger" as the Jews and "those who are astray" as the Christians, given that the two attributes of anger and error accompany each other?

The answer: this is not a restriction that implies the negation of each attribute from the people of the other attribute. For every one who has earned anger is astray, and every one who is astray has earned anger. Rather, each group is named by the most prominent and most fitting of the two attributes, the one most closely attached to it, and this is the attribute that predominates over them. This agrees with God's description of the Jews with anger in the Qur'an and of the Christians with error. So it is an interpretation of the verse by the attribute with which He described them in that passage. As for the Jews, God Most High says of them: "Wretched is that for which they have sold their souls, that they should disbelieve in what God has revealed, out of resentment that God should send down of His bounty upon whom He wills of His servants. So they have returned burdened with anger upon anger, and for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment." Regarding the repetition of this anger here, there are several opinions. The first: it is a repeated anger in return for their repeated disbelief in the Messenger of God (ﷺ), their transgression against him, and their fighting him. So they deserved one anger for their disbelief, and another anger for their transgression and their turning away from him. A parallel to this is God's words: "Those who disbelieved and barred from the way of God, We will increase their punishment upon punishment." So the first punishment was for their disbelief, and the punishment He added to them was for their barring people from His way. The second opinion: the first anger is for their distortion, alteration, and killing of the prophets, and the second anger is for their disbelief in Christ. The third opinion: the first anger is for their disbelief in Christ, and the second anger is for their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ). The correct view regarding the verse is that the repetition here does not mean duplication that doubles a single thing, but rather anger after anger, in accordance with the repetition of their disbelief, their corruption, their killing of the prophets, their disbelief in Christ and in Muhammad (ﷺ), their enmity toward the messengers of God, and other deeds, each of which requires anger in its own right. This is like His words: "Then return the gaze; do you see any flaw? Then return the gaze twice," meaning return again and again, not merely twice. The intention of multiplicity in His words "they have returned burdened with anger upon anger" is clearer. There is no doubt that their suspension of what they neglected of the laws of the Torah, along with their distortion and alteration, requires anger; their denial of the prophets requires another anger; their killing of them requires another anger; their denial of Christ, their plot to kill him, and their accusing his mother of a great calumny require anger; their denial of the Prophet (ﷺ) requires anger; their hostility toward him and their harm to his followers require anger; and their barring those who wished to enter his religion from it requires anger. So they are the people of anger, may God preserve us from His anger. They are the people who returned with the doubled and repeated anger of God, and they were more deserving of this name and attribute than the Christians. God Most High said regarding them: "Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as a recompense from God? Those whom God cursed and with whom He was angry, and of whom He made apes and swine, and who served the false deity." This is anger accompanied by curse and transformation, which is the most intense form of anger. And God Most High said: "Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed by the tongue of David and Jesus son of Mary, because they disobeyed and used to transgress. They did not forbid one another from any wrong they committed; wretched indeed was what they used to do. You see many of them allying with those who disbelieved. Wretched is what their souls have sent forward for them, that God has become angry with them, and in the punishment they will abide." As for the description of the Christians with error, it is in His words: "Say: O People of the Book, do not exceed the bounds in your religion beyond the truth, and do not follow the desires of a people who had gone astray before and led many astray, and who strayed from the right way." This is an address to the Christians, because it is in the context of His address to them with His words: "Certainly those have disbelieved who say that God is the Messiah, son of Mary, and the Messiah said, 'O Children of Israel, worship God, my Lord and your Lord,'" up to His words, "and they strayed from the right way." So He described them as having gone astray first and then led many astray, and these are their followers. This refers to the time before the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, when they went astray regarding the matter of the Messiah and led their followers astray. When the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, they increased in another error by denying him and disbelieving in him. So the error was multiplied in their case. This is the view of a group among them, al-Zamakhshari and others, and it is weak. For all of this is a description of their predecessors, whom these people follow. So He described them with three attributes: first, that they had gone astray before them; second, that they led their followers astray; and third, that they strayed from the right way. These are attributes of their predecessors, whose desires these people were forbidden to follow. So it cannot be a description of those who were present in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), because they are themselves the ones addressed by the prohibition, not those prohibited from following. So reflect on it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 1, verse 7 (part 7 of 8):

The secret of the verse is that it implies the repetition of misguidance concerning the Christians, one misguidance after another, because of the extent of their ignorance of the truth. It is parallel to the verse mentioned earlier concerning the repetition of anger regarding the Jews. For this reason, the Christians are more specifically associated with misguidance than the Jews. The reason this misguidance is repeated is that misguidance may miss its very aim, so the person is astray in the goal itself. He then seeks what he should not seek and worships what he should not worship. Or he may reach a true aim but go astray in the path and the means that lead to it. The first is misguidance in the end, and the second is misguidance in the means. Then, if he calls others to that, he has led them astray. The predecessors of the Christians combined all three types. They went astray from their aim, since they did not attain it, and they claimed that their god was a human who eats, drinks, weeps, was killed, crucified and slapped. This is misguidance in the aim itself, since they did not achieve it, and they went astray from the path that leads to it. So they were not guided to the goal or to the way that leads to it. They called their followers to this, and so they went astray from the truth and from its path, and they led many astray. Thus they were more deeply immersed in misguidance than the Jews, and they were described by the more specific of the two descriptions.

What confirms this is that the Jews came about through corrupt will, envy, and preferring what they had over their people, such as illicit gains and leadership. They feared that Islam would take these away from them. They were not afflicted by a lack of knowledge of the truth, for they knew that Muhammad (ﷺ) was the Messenger of God just as they knew their own sons. For this reason God did not rebuke them and reprimand them except for their corrupt intentions: arrogance, envy, preferring illicit gain, transgression, and killing the prophets. He rebuked the Christians with misguidance and ignorance, which is the lack of knowledge of the truth. Wretchedness and disbelief arise from failing to know the truth at times, and from failing to will it and act upon it at other times, and they combine. So the disbelief of the Jews arose from not willing the truth and acting upon it, and from preferring something else over it after knowing it. Thus it was not pure misguidance. The disbelief of the Christians arose from their ignorance of the truth and their going astray regarding it. When it becomes clear to them and they prefer falsehood over it, they resemble the people of anger and remain "those who have earned anger and are astray."

Then, since guidance, success and felicity cannot be attained except by knowing the truth and preferring it over other things, and since ignorance prevents the servant from knowing the truth and transgression prevents him from willing it, the servant is most in need of asking God at all times to guide him to the straight path. This means guidance through instruction, clarification, direction, inspiration, enablement, and help, so that He teaches him, makes him know, then makes him desire it and intend to follow it. Thus he leaves the way of those who have earned anger, who deviated from it deliberately and knowingly, and the way of those who went astray, who deviated from it through ignorance and misguidance. The predecessors used to say: "Whoever among our scholars is corrupt has a resemblance to the Jews, and whoever among our worshippers is corrupt has a resemblance to the Christians." This is as they said. Whoever among the scholars becomes corrupt and adopts the character of the Jews, such as distorting words from their places, concealing what God has revealed when it defeats his aim, envying those whom God has granted of His bounty, seeking to kill them, killing people who enjoin justice and call them to the Book of their Lord and the Sunnah of their Prophet, and other characters for which the Jews were condemned, such as disbelief, twisting the tongue, concealment, distortion, employing tricks to get forbidden things, and mixing truth with falsehood, then his resemblance to the Jews is clear. As for whoever among the worshippers becomes corrupt and worships according to his desires rather than what His Messenger (ﷺ) was sent with, and exaggerates regarding the shaykhs, placing them at the level of lordship, and goes beyond that to some form of incarnation (hulul) or unity (ittihad), then his resemblance to the Christians is clear. So the Muslim must keep as far away as possible from these two resemblances.
