Whoever contemplates these two resemblances and two descriptions and knows the conditions of people knows the necessity of this supplication and his need for it. There is no supplication more beneficial for the servant, nor one more obligatory for him. His need for it is greater than his need for life and soul, because the most that can be lost by losing them is death, whereas by losing this he suffers the wretchedness of eternity. So we ask God to guide us to the straight path, the path of those You have blessed, not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray. Amen. Indeed He is near and responsive.

[Section: The placing of ﴿those who have earned anger﴾ before ﴿those who are astray﴾]

As for the thirteenth issue, namely the placing of "those who have earned anger" before "those who are astray," there are several reasons.

First: they precede them in time.

Second: they were the ones closest to the Prophet (ﷺ) among the People of the Two Scriptures, for they were his neighbours in Medina, whereas the Christians' dwellings were far from him. For this reason you find that the address to the Jews and speaking with them in the noble Qur'an is more frequent than the address to the Christians, as in Surat al-Baqarah, al-Ma'idah, Al 'Imran and others.

Third: the Jews were more severe in disbelief than the Christians. For this reason anger, curse and punishment were more specific to them, since their disbelief was out of obstinacy and transgression, as has been mentioned. Thus warning against their path and distancing from it is more deserving and more important to be placed first. The punishment of one who is ignorant is not like the punishment of one who knows.

Fourth, and it is the best of them: the blessed ones were mentioned before, and anger is the opposite of blessing. The surah is "the seven oft-repeated" (al-sab' al-mathani), in which a thing is mentioned together with its opposite. Mentioning "those who have earned anger" alongside "those whom You have blessed" carries a pairing and contrast that is absent in placing "those who are astray" there. Your saying "people are blessed and angered, so be among the blessed" is better than your saying "blessed and astray." He used the passive participle for "angered" and the active participle for "astray."

[Section]

As for the fourteenth issue, namely that for the people of anger the passive participle is used, and for "those who are astray" the active participle is used:

The answer to both is clear. The people of anger are those upon whom God's anger was directed and fell, so they are "those upon whom anger has been earned."

As for the people of misguidance, they are those who went astray, preferred misguidance, and acquired it. For this reason they deserve punishment for it. It is not fitting to say "wa-la al-mudallin" in the passive, because there is in its implication the excusing of them and the suggestion that they did not acquire misguidance from themselves, but that it was done to them. There is no proof in this for the Qadariyya (those who deny divine decree), for we say that they are the ones who went astray, even though God had led them astray. Rather, the verse is a refutation of the Jabriyya (those who attribute no act to the servant except in a metaphorical rather than a literal sense). Thus the verse includes a refutation of them, just as the phrase "guide us to the straight path" includes a refutation of the Qadariyya. So in the verse is the nullification of the two groups' views, and a testimony for the people of truth that they are the ones who are correct. They affirm divine decree in terms of tawhid and creation, and they affirm the servant's power by ascribing the acts of the servants to them in terms of action and acquisition (kasb), and this is the object of command and action, just as the former is the object of creation and power. Thus the verse establishes the sharia, the decree, the resurrection and prophethood. Blessing and anger are its reward and punishment. The blessed ones are none other than His messengers and their followers, and the guidance of their followers occurs through them. So it establishes prophethood by the nearest and clearest way, and the one most indicative of the universal need for it and the severity of necessity for it. The servant cannot be among the blessed except by God's guidance to him, and this guidance is not attained except through the messengers. This guidance has a fruit, which is the complete and absolute blessing in the Abode of Bliss. Its opposite also has a fruit, which is the anger that entails everlasting wretchedness. Reflect how this verse, despite its brevity and conciseness, contains the most important and most glorious aims of religion. God is the Guide to the right path, and He knows best.

[Section]

As for the fifteenth issue, namely what is the purpose of the added "la" (not) between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined:

There are four benefits in it.

The first: its mention emphasizes the negation implied by the word "ghayr" (other than). Had it not been for the negative sense in it, it would not have been conjoined with "la" and the conjunction "wa." So it is in the sense of "neither those who have earned anger nor those who are astray," or "other than those who have earned anger and other than those who are astray."

The second benefit: the intended meaning is the difference between the two types and between each type taken individually. If "la" were not mentioned and it were said "other than those who have earned anger and those who are astray," it would give the impression that what is meant is what differs from the combined group of the two types, not what differs from each type individually. But when it is said "wa la al-dallin," it is explicit that the intended path is other than these and other than these. The explanation is that if you say "Zayd and 'Amr did not stand," you have negated standing from both of them, but this does not entail negating it from each one individually.

The third benefit: to remove the suspicion that "those who are astray" is a descriptive adjective of "those who have earned anger," and that they are one category described by anger and misguidance, with the conjunction between them coming as it does in the conjunction of attributes with one another. Examples include God's saying: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded, those who are humble in their prayer, and those who turn away from idle talk﴾ to the end, for these are the attributes of the believers. Another example is His saying: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, and who decreed and guided﴾ and similar verses. When "la" entered, it was known that they are two distinct categories intended for mention. "La" was more appropriate for this meaning than "ghayr" for several reasons:

First: it has fewer letters.

Second: it avoids repetition of the word.

Third: the heaviness resulting from pronouncing "ghayr" twice without separation except by a single word, and there is no doubt that this is heavy on the tongue.

Fourth: "la" is only used for conjunction after a negation, so bringing it indicates the negation of anger from the people of the straight path, just as misguidance was negated from them. "Ghayr," although it conveys this, is no more emphatic in negation than "la." This is how the answer to the sixteenth issue is known, namely that "la" is only used for conjunction in negation.

[Section]

As for the seventeenth issue, namely: which of the types of guidance is meant here?

Know that the types of guidance are four.

The first is the general guidance shared by all creatures, mentioned in God's saying: ﴿Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation, then guided it﴾. That is, He gave everything its form by which it is not confused with anything else, gave every limb its shape and configuration, gave every existing thing its specific nature, and then guided it to the works for which it was created. This is the guidance of the animal that moves by its own will to bring what benefits it and repel what harms it. It is also the guidance of the non-living things subjected to their purposes. Each has a guidance fitting to it, just as each kind of animal has a guidance fitting to it, though their kinds and forms differ. Likewise each limb has a guidance fitting to it: He guided the two legs to walking, the hands to grasping and working, the tongue to speech, the ear to hearing, the eye to seeing visible things, and each limb to what it was created for. He guided the two sexes of every animal to pairing and reproduction and raising offspring, and He guided the infant to seize the breast at birth and to seek it. The degrees of His guidance, glory be to Him, cannot be counted except by Him. Blessed is God, Lord of the worlds.

He guided the bee to take homes from the mountains, from trees and from buildings, then to follow the paths of its Lord, made submissive to it, not resisting it. Then it returns to its homes, and He guided it to obey and follow its leader wherever he directs it. Then He guided it to build the wondrously crafted and firmly constructed houses. Whoever reflects on some of His guidance manifested in the world bears witness that He is God, there is no god but Him, Knower of the unseen and the seen, the Mighty, the Wise. From knowledge of this guidance, one moves to establishing prophethood by the easiest reflection, at first glance, by the best and shortest path, and the one furthest from every doubt. For He did not leave these animals purposeless or idle, but guided them to this guidance which the intellects of the intelligent cannot comprehend. How could it be fitting for Him to leave the human species, which is the essence of existence, which He honoured and preferred over many of His creatures, purposeless, idle and unattended, not guiding it to its utmost perfections and best ends, leaving it idle, not commanding it, not forbidding it, not rewarding it, not punishing it? Is this not contrary to His wisdom and an attribution to Him that is unfitting to His majesty? For this reason He denounced such a belief in those who held it and declared Himself exalted above it, and He explained that such an attribution to Him is impossible and that He is far above it. He said, exalted is He: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ ﴿So exalted is God, the true King﴾. He declared Himself free of this supposition, which indicates that its falsehood is established in sound natures and upright intellects. This is one of the things that proves the resurrection by reason, and that it is something on which reason and revelation both agree, and it is the sounder of the two approaches in this matter. Whoever understands this understands the secret of the juxtaposition of His saying: ﴿There is no creature on earth, nor bird that flies with its two wings, but they are communities like you. We have not neglected anything in the Book. Then to their Lord they will be gathered﴾ with His saying: ﴿They say: Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord? Say: Indeed God is able to send down a sign, but most of them do not know﴾. And how this came in the context of their answer to this question, with a reference to establishing prophethood, and that He who has not neglected the affair of every creature on earth or bird that flies with its wings, but made them communities and guided them to their ends and their interests, how would He not guide you to your perfection and your interests? So this is one type of guidance, and the most general of them.

The second type: the guidance of explanation, indication and instruction, to show the two paths of good and evil and the two ways of salvation and ruin. This guidance does not necessarily entail complete guidance, for it is a cause and a condition, not a determining factor. For this reason, guidance is ascribed along with it, as in His saying: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾. That is, We made clear to them, directed them and showed them, but they were not guided. Among its examples is His saying: ﴿And indeed you guide to a straight path﴾.

The third type: the guidance of success (tawfiq) and inspiration (ilham), which is the guidance that necessarily results in being guided, so it is never separated from it. It is mentioned in His saying: ﴿He leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾, and in His saying: ﴿If you are eager for their guidance, then indeed God does not guide those who lead astray﴾.

And in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whomever God guides, none can misguide him, and whomever He misguides, none can guide him." Narrated by Muslim, Ahmad and al-Bayhaqi.

And in His saying: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾. Thus He negated this guidance from him and affirmed for him the guidance of calling and explanation in His saying: ﴿And indeed you guide to a straight path﴾.

The fourth type: the ultimate outcome of this guidance, which is the guidance to Paradise and Hell when their people are driven to them. God said: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, their Lord will guide them by their faith. Rivers will flow beneath them in Gardens of Bliss﴾. The people of Paradise will say therein: ﴿Praise be to God who guided us to this﴾. And God said of the people of the Fire: ﴿Gather those who did wrong and their companions and what they used to worship besides God, and guide them to the path of Hellfire﴾.

Having known this, the guidance requested in His saying: ﴿the straight path﴾ encompasses only the second and third types in particular. It is a request for instruction, clarification, direction, success and inspiration. It is a request for instruction, clarification and success.

If it is said: how is one asking for instruction and clarification when it is already attained for him, and likewise inspiration and success?

We say: this has been answered by saying that what is meant is firmness and the continuation of guidance.

Know that the servant does not attain complete guidance, which is what is sought, except after six matters, of which he has an absolute need and from which he has no independence. The first matter: that he knows, in all that he does and refrains from, that he is loved by the Lord, exalted, and pleasing to Him, so he prefers it, and that he is hated by Him and displeasing to Him, so he avoids it. If some of this knowledge and recognition is lacking, some of his complete guidance is lacking in proportion to it. The second matter: that he wills all that God loves him to do, resolving upon it, and wills to abandon everything God has forbidden, resolving to abandon it once it occurs to his mind in detail, and resolving to abandon it in general terms. If some of his will for this is lacking, some of complete guidance is lacking in proportion to the lack of will. The third matter: that he practises it in action and in abstention. If some of his action is lacking, some of his guidance is lacking in proportion. These are three principles of guidance, and three further things follow from them that complete and perfect it:

The first: matters to which he was guided in general, but not to their details, so he needs guidance to their details.

The second: matters to which he was guided from one aspect but not another, so he needs complete guidance in them, so that his guidance in them may be perfected.

The first part of this passage is Ibn al-Qayyim's discussion of the seventh verse of al-Fatihah, and it ends with a separate section on saying "Amin" aloud in prayer.

Part 8 of 8 begins with the third category: matters that guidance has been granted in detail from all their aspects. The servant needs to persist in that guidance and remain steadfast upon it. These are principles that relate to what he resolves to do or to leave undone. The seventh matter relates to the past: things that occurred from him in a manner other than the straight path. He needs to remedy them by repenting from them and replacing them with something else. If that is the case, it may be asked: how can he ask for guidance when he already has it? The answer is that what is intended is firmness and persistence in it. When these levels are already attained by him in actuality, his asking for guidance becomes a request for firmness and continuance. However, when what he is ignorant of far outweighs what he knows, and what he does not will of his own rightful conduct is more than what he wills, and he has no way to act upon it except that God creates the one who acts within him, then what is requested is the very origin of guidance, its continuance, by teaching, granting success, creating the will within him, enabling him, creating the capacity to act, and making him firm upon that. It is thus known that there is no greater necessity for him than to ask for guidance: its origin and its details, in knowledge and action, its firmness, and its continuance until death. The secret of this is that the servant is in need of guidance at every breath, in all that he does and leaves undone, in its origin and in its details, and in its firmness, and he is in need of an increase in knowledge of the guidance on an ongoing basis. There is nothing more beneficial to him, and nothing he is more in need of, than asking for guidance. So we ask God to guide us to the straight path and to make our hearts firm upon His religion.

(Section)

As for the nineteenth question: it concerns the use of the plural pronoun in His words ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾. Some people have answered this by saying that every limb of the servant and every sense, outward and inward, requires a specific guidance of its own, so the plural form was used, treating each limb as one seeking guidance and asking for its own guidance. I presented this answer to Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may God sanctify his spirit, and he considered it very weak. He said, and he was right: "The human being is a name for the whole, not for each part of his body and each limb of it." The one who says, "Forgive me, have mercy on me, mend me, set me right, and guide me," is asking God for what accrues to his whole, outward and inward, and he does not need to sense a separate request for each limb, for which he would use a distinct wording. The correct view is that this agrees with His words ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾. Using the plural pronoun in both places is better and more dignified, because the context is one of servitude, dependence upon the Lord, the Exalted, and acknowledgment of need for His servanthood, His help, and His guidance. So He used the plural form, meaning: we, the company of Your servants, confess to You our servitude. This is like a servant saying to a great king: "We are Your servants and Your slaves, under Your obedience, and we do not oppose Your command." This is better and of greater standing with the king than saying, "I am Your servant and Your slave." For this reason, if one were to say, "I alone am Your slave," he would invite the king's anger. But if he says, "I and everyone in the city are Your slaves, Your servants, and Your soldiers," it is greater and more dignified, because it implies that Your servants are very numerous and I am one of them, and we all share in Your servitude, in seeking Your help, and in asking You for guidance. Thus it includes praise of the Lord for the breadth of His glory and the multitude of His servants and of those who ask Him for guidance, which the singular form does not convey. Reflect upon this.

If you reflect upon the supplications of the Qur'an, you will see that most of them follow this pattern, such as ﴿Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾, and similar supplications at the end of al-Baqarah, at the end and beginning of Al 'Imran, and most of the supplications of the Noble Qur'an.

(Section)

The twentieth question: what is "the straight path" (al-sirat al-mustaqim)?

Here we mention a brief statement, since people's expressions about it have varied, and their renderings of it differ according to its attributes, its relations, and its reality. Yet the reality is one thing: it is the path of God, which He has specified for His servants through the tongues of His messengers, which He made a means for His servants to reach Him, and for which there is no other route to Him for them. Rather, all other roads are closed except this one. It consists of singling Him out in worship and singling out His Messenger in obedience. So one does not associate anyone with Him in His worship, nor associate anyone with His Messenger in obedience. Thus one purifies the monotheism and purifies the following of the Messenger. This is the meaning of the saying of some of the knowers: "Happiness and success are all combined in two things: sincere love for Him and good conduct toward Him." All of this is contained in the testimony that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Whatever the path has been explained as, it falls within these two foundations. The essence of this and its binding principle is that you love Him with your whole heart and please Him with your whole effort, so that there is no place in your heart except one filled with His love, and you have no will except one directed toward His pleasure. The first is attained through the realization of the testimony that there is no god but God, and the second is attained through the realization of the testimony that Muhammad is the Messenger of God. This is the Guide and the religion of truth. It is the knowledge of the truth and acting for it, which is knowing what God sent His messengers with and upholding it. So say whatever expressions you like, of which this is the best and the pivot of the millstone. It is the meaning of the saying of one who said: "Knowledge and outward and inward deeds derived from the niche of prophethood," and the meaning of the saying of one who said: "Following the Messenger of God (ﷺ) outwardly and inwardly, in knowledge and in action," and the meaning of the saying of one who said: "Affirming to God His oneness and steadfastness upon His command." As for what is other than this among the sayings, such as the saying of one who said: "The five prayers," and the saying of one who said: "Love for Abu Bakr and Umar," and the saying of one who said: "It is the five pillars of Islam upon which it is built," all these sayings are examples and varieties, not an exact explanation of it. Rather, they are parts of it, and its comprehensive reality is what has preceded.

And God knows best.

[Saying "Amin" Aloud in Prayer]

Abandoning the established, authentic Sunnah regarding saying "Amin" aloud in prayer. As in his saying in the two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim): "When the imam says 'Amin,' then say 'Amin,' for whoever's saying of 'Amin' coincides with the saying of the angels, his previous sins will be forgiven."

Had he not said it aloud, it would not have been possible for the follower to say "Amin" along with him and to match him in saying it.

Even more explicit than this is the hadith of Sufyan al-Thawri from Salamah ibn Kuhayl, from Hujr ibn Anbas, from Wa'il ibn Hujr, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) would, when he said 'nor of those who are astray,' say 'Amin,' and he raised his voice with it."

In another wording: "and he prolonged it."

Narrated by al-Tirmidhi and others, and its chain is sahih (authentic).

Shu'bah, however, differed from Sufyan in this hadith, saying: "and he lowered his voice with it."

The judgment of the imams of hadith and its memorizers in this matter favors Sufyan. Al-Tirmidhi said: I heard Muhammad ibn Isma'il (al-Bukhari) say: "The hadith of Sufyan al-Thawri from Salamah ibn Kuhayl on this subject is more authentic than the hadith of Shu'bah. Shu'bah erred in this hadith in several places: he said, 'from Hujr Abi al-Anbas,' whereas his kunyah is Abu al-Sakan, and he added 'Alqamah ibn Wa'il' to it, whereas it is Hujr ibn Anbas from Wa'il ibn Hujr, with no mention of Alqamah. And he said, 'and he lowered his voice with it.'"

The correct position is that he said it aloud.

Al-Tirmidhi said: I asked Abu Zur'ah about this hadith of Sufyan and Shu'bah, and he said: "The hadith of Sufyan is more authentic than the hadith of Shu'bah. Al-'Ala' ibn Salih also narrated from Salamah ibn Kuhayl something similar to the narration of Sufyan."

Al-Daraqutni said: "Shu'bah said, 'and he lowered his voice with it.' It is said that he erred in this, because Sufyan al-Thawri, Muhammad ibn Salamah ibn Kuhayl, and others narrated it from Salamah, saying: 'and he raised his voice with "Amin."'" This is the correct position.

Al-Bayhaqi said: "I know of no disagreement among the people of hadith knowledge that when Sufyan and Shu'bah differ, the statement of Sufyan is to be preferred." Yahya ibn Sa'id said: "No one is more beloved to me than Shu'bah, and no one is more just in my view than him. When Sufyan differs from him, I take the statement of Sufyan." Shu'bah himself said: "Sufyan has a better memory than I do." This is one preponderance for the narration of Sufyan.

A second preponderance is the corroboration of al-'Ala' ibn Salih and Muhammad ibn Salamah ibn Kuhayl for it.

A third preponderance is that Abu al-Walid al-Tayalisi, and you have him as a witness, narrated from Shu'bah in agreement with al-Thawri in its text. The narration from Shu'bah has been varied, as you see.

Al-Bayhaqi said: "It is possible that he became alert to this and returned to the correct text, and that Alqamah's mention in the chain was dropped."

A fourth preponderance is that if the two narrations were equal in weight, the narration that includes raising the voice contains an addition, and an addition is more deserving of acceptance.

A fifth preponderance is that it agrees with and explains the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "When the imam says 'Amin,' then say 'Amin,' for the imam says 'Amin' and the angels say 'Amin,' so whoever's saying of 'Amin' coincides with the saying of the angels will be forgiven."

A sixth preponderance is what al-Hakim narrated with a sahih chain from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) finished reciting Umm al-Qur'an (al-Fatihah), he raised his voice with 'Amin.'" Abu Dawud has a similar narration with more explanation: "He said 'Amin' until those in the first row near him could hear." In another narration from him: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) said, 'not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray,' he would say 'Amin,' raising his voice with it, and he would order that."

Al-Bayhaqi mentioned from Ali, may God honor his face, who said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say 'Amin' when he recited, 'not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray.'"

Also from him, may God be pleased with him: "The Prophet (ﷺ) would, when he recited 'nor of those who are astray,' raise his voice with 'Amin.'"

In Abu Dawud, from Bilal, who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do not precede me with 'Amin.'"

Al-Rabi' said: Al-Shafi'i was asked about the imam: "Does he raise his voice with 'Amin'?" He said: "Yes, and those behind him raise their voices with it." I said: "What is the proof?" He said: "Malik informed us," and he mentioned the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, whose authenticity is agreed upon, and then said: "In the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), 'When the imam says "Amin," then say "Amin,"' there is an indication that he ordered the imam to say 'Amin' aloud, because those behind him cannot know the time of their saying 'Amin' unless they hear his saying of it." Then Ibn Shihab clarified it, saying: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to say, 'Amin.'" I said to al-Shafi'i: "We dislike for the imam to raise his voice with 'Amin.'" He said: "This is contrary to what our companion and your companion narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Even if we and they had no knowledge other than this hadith which we mentioned from Malik, it would be proper to infer that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say 'Amin' aloud and that he ordered the imam to say it aloud. How then, when the people of knowledge have always acted upon it?"

Wa'il ibn Hujr narrated that "the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say 'Amin,' raising his voice with it," and he would draw out its pronunciation.

Abu Hurayrah used to say to the imam: "Do not precede me with 'Amin.'" He would also call the adhan for him. Muslim ibn Khalid informed us from Ibn Jurayj, from Ata': "I used to hear the imams, Ibn al-Zubayr and those after him, say 'Amin,' and those behind them say 'Amin,' until the mosque would echo."

His statement, "Abu Hurayrah used to say to the imam, do not precede me with 'Amin,'" refers to what al-Bayhaqi mentioned with his chain from Abu Rafi', that Abu Hurayrah used to call the adhan for Marwan ibn al-Hakam, and he stipulated that Marwan should not precede him with "nor of those who are astray" until he knew that he had reached the row. So when Marwan said, "﴿nor of those who are astray﴾" [al-Fatihah: 7], Abu Hurayrah would say "Amin," drawing out his voice with it, and he said: "When the 'Amin' of the people of the earth coincides with the 'Amin' of the people of heaven, they will be forgiven." Ata' said: "I encountered two hundred companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in this mosque, and when the imam said, '﴿not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray﴾' [al-Fatihah: 7], I heard from them a roar of 'Amin.'"

All of this is refuted by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾ [al-A'raf: 204]. The one to whom this verse was revealed is the one who raised his voice with the saying of "Amin," and those who were commanded with it raised their voices with it. There is no contradiction whatsoever between the verse and the Sunnah.
